stories.title: Oscar Piastri steals pole from Norris by 0.012s for Verstappen's final home race grid
stories.what_happened: In qualifying for Sunday's Dutch Grand Prix, Oscar Piastri edged out his McLaren teammate Lando Norris by a mere 0.012 seconds to claim pole position, capping a tense back-and-forth qualifying duel between the two title-contending drivers. Max Verstappen qualified third for what is being treated as his emotional final home race at Zandvoort, with the circuit set to leave the F1 calendar after this event. Red Bull's Isack Hadjar produced the surprise of the session, qualifying fourth — a career-best result for the 20-year-old rookie, who had endured a difficult Friday practice before finding his form. Norris, who had been fastest in every practice session across the weekend, said the margin came down to a small headwind on his final Q3 lap that cost him around one-hundredth of a second, calling the result partly a matter of luck given the changing wind conditions at the seaside circuit.
key_points: **Oscar Piastri** beat McLaren teammate **Lando Norris** to pole for Sunday's Dutch Grand Prix by just **0.012 seconds**.
**Max Verstappen** starts **third** at his emotional last home race, with Zandvoort set to **drop off the F1 calendar** after this weekend.
**Isack Hadjar** produced a **shock fourth-place** qualifying lap, the best result of the **20-year-old rookie's** career so far.
Norris had **topped every practice session** at Zandvoort but couldn't convert that pace into pole, blaming a **headwind on his final lap**.

depth.background: Zandvoort's Dutch Grand Prix returned to the Formula 1 calendar in 2021 after a more than three-decade absence, quickly becoming a fan favorite for its narrow, banked layout and passionate crowds cheering on Max Verstappen, F1's most successful Dutch driver. This is confirmed to be Zandvoort's last race on the current calendar, adding extra emotional weight for Verstappen and the crowd. Going into this weekend, McLaren's Norris and Piastri have been locked in a tight championship fight, trading practice and qualifying pace all season.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty snap a six-day winning streak as investors turn cautious ahead of Powell's Jackson Hole speech
stories.what_happened: Indian benchmark indices closed lower on **Friday, August 22**, ending a six-day winning streak. The **Sensex** settled at 81,306.85, down 693.86 points or 0.85%, while the **Nifty 50** fell 213.65 points, also 0.85%, to close at 24,870.10. The decline was broad-based: 25 of the Sensex's 30 constituent stocks fell, including heavyweights like **HDFC Bank, TCS, ICICI Bank, Asian Paints and Tech Mahindra**, down as much as 2%. Sector-wise, metals, PSU banks and private banks led the losses, falling over 1% each. The pullback followed a sharp rally earlier in the week driven by GST-reform optimism, but for the week as a whole the indices still ended around 1% higher.
key_points: Sensex fell **693.86 points (0.85%)** to close at 81,306.85; Nifty 50 dropped **213.65 points (0.85%)** to 24,870.10.
The fall **snapped a six-session rally** that had been fuelled by optimism over India's GST reforms.
Selling was broad-based, with **25 of 30 Sensex stocks** trading lower, including HDFC Bank, TCS and ICICI Bank.
Investors turned cautious ahead of Fed Chair **Jerome Powell's Jackson Hole speech** later Friday, which markets watch for interest-rate hints.
Despite Friday's drop, both indices still ended the **week roughly 1% higher**.

depth.background: Indian markets had been on a strong run this week, lifted by optimism that the government's push to simplify **GST (Goods and Services Tax)** into just two slabs would boost consumption, plus hopes of a possible **credit-rating upgrade** from S&P. That rally ran into a wall of caution as traders positioned ahead of the **Jackson Hole Symposium** — an annual gathering of central bankers in Wyoming, US — where the Federal Reserve chair's speech is scrutinised for clues on the future path of US interest rates. Since global bond yields and Fed policy directly influence how much foreign money flows into or out of emerging markets like India, uncertainty ahead of that speech is enough to trigger profit-taking.

stories.title: Hamilton crashes out of the Zandvoort sprint and is hit with a grid penalty for next week's Italian GP
stories.what_happened: During Saturday's sprint race weekend at Zandvoort, Hamilton **crashed out** of the sprint through what stewards attributed to his own driver error. Separately, he was handed a **five-place grid penalty** for next weekend's Italian Grand Prix at Monza for failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags on his way to the grid before the session, plus **two penalty points** added to his superlicence. Because the penalty is being served at Monza rather than Zandvoort, Hamilton will start no higher than sixth at Ferrari's home race — a event with huge symbolic weight for the Italian team and its passionate fanbase (the 'tifosi').
key_points: Hamilton **crashed out** of the Dutch GP sprint at Zandvoort through his own driver error.
He was separately handed a **five-place grid penalty** for failing to slow for yellow flags on the way to the grid.
The penalty applies at **Monza**, Ferrari's home race, next weekend — he'll start **no higher than 6th**.
He also picked up **two penalty points** on his superlicence.
It deepens a rocky sprint weekend for Ferrari's title bid after a difficult new-chassis debut.

depth.background: Lewis Hamilton joined **Ferrari** for the 2026 season chasing a first title with the sport's most storied team, but the year has been bumpier than hoped, with reliability and setup issues cropping up at points during the campaign. Zandvoort's **sprint format** weekend gives drivers less practice time to dial in the car before a short sprint race and sprint qualifying feed into the grid, raising the stakes of even small mistakes. A driver's **superlicence** carries a penalty-points system — reach 12 within a rolling 12-month window and it triggers an automatic race ban, so points added now matter cumulatively across the season.

stories.title: FIA stewards investigate Carlos Sainz over 'driving unnecessarily slowly' in Zandvoort sprint qualifying
stories.what_happened: Following **sprint qualifying** at the Dutch Grand Prix, FIA race stewards opened a formal investigation into Williams driver **Carlos Sainz** over an alleged breach of driving unnecessarily slowly during the session. It came in a weekend already busy for the stewards' room: **Max Verstappen** was separately summoned over an alleged overtake under red-flag conditions during Friday's second practice session, but was cleared with **no further action** after explaining the incident. The Sainz case remains under review, with any penalty potentially affecting his starting position for the sprint race or Sunday's Grand Prix.
key_points: Williams driver **Carlos Sainz** is under FIA investigation following sprint qualifying at Zandvoort.
The probe centres on an allegation he was **driving unnecessarily slowly** during the session.
It's one of several steward inquiries at the Dutch GP weekend, alongside a separate Verstappen probe over an FP2 red-flag incident.
Verstappen was cleared with **no further action** after his own hearing.
A penalty for Sainz could affect his **grid position** for the sprint or main race.

depth.background: 'Driving unnecessarily slowly' is a regulatory category F1 stewards use when a driver appears to deliberately back off on track in a way that could disrupt other drivers' laps — often during qualifying, when cars are on out-laps or cool-down laps and track position matters enormously for getting a clean run at a fast lap. **Zandvoort's** narrow, high-speed layout makes such incidents more consequential than at wider circuits, since there's little room for cars to pass a slow-moving car safely.

stories.title: Justice Sanjay Karol retires from the Supreme Court after a term marked by access-to-justice rulings
stories.what_happened: Justice Sanjay Karol formally retired from the Supreme Court of India on **August 22, 2026**, closing out a three-and-a-half-year tenure on the top court. The **Supreme Court Bar Association** and the **Supreme Court Advocates-on-Record Association** each held farewell functions in his honour. Chief Justice Surya Kant praised his commitment to 'accessibility and institutional dignity,' noting the bench loses 'an officer who combined administrative reform with a human approach to litigation.' Over his career, Justice Karol authored more than 270 judgements, including a landmark Patna High Court ruling that recognised access to clean public toilets as a **fundamental right**, and he is credited with more than halving pending cases during his time as Tripura's Chief Justice.
key_points: Justice Sanjay Karol demitted office from the **Supreme Court of India on August 22**, after a **three-and-a-half-year tenure**.
He authored **over 270 judgements**, including a Patna High Court ruling recognising **access to clean toilets as a fundamental right**.
As Chief Justice of Tripura, he helped **cut case pendency by more than half**.
Chief Justice **Surya Kant** praised him as 'a judge who lived the Constitution' at his farewell.
He is one of **five Supreme Court judges retiring in 2026**, part of a broader generational turnover on the bench.

depth.background: India's Supreme Court judges retire mandatorily at **age 65**, and 2026 is a year with an unusually large number of retirements reshaping the court's composition. Justice Karol rose through the Himachal Pradesh High Court before serving as **Chief Justice of Tripura and Patna High Courts**, then was elevated to the Supreme Court, where he built a reputation for rulings that connected constitutional principles to everyday, practical access-to-justice issues rather than only high-profile political cases.

stories.title: IMD issues heavy rain warnings across 20 states as monsoon intensifies — from Punjab to the Northeast
stories.what_happened: The India Meteorological Department issued heavy rainfall warnings on Saturday covering roughly 20 states as monsoon activity intensified across northern, central, and northeastern India. Delhi, Chandigarh, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, and Jammu & Kashmir are all under warning, alongside Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Madhya Pradesh, Odisha, sub-Himalayan West Bengal, Sikkim, and the seven northeastern states. Unlike a single national holiday order, closure decisions are made locally — individual states, districts, or even schools issue their own notices, so the same warning can mean a shutdown in one district and business-as-usual in the next. Separately, the IMD has flagged that Mumbai's metro region — Thane, Palghar, and Raigad — should expect a fresh orange alert for heavy-to-very-heavy rain starting August 24, meaning this isn't an isolated spell but part of an active, moving monsoon system.
key_points: India's weather office (**IMD**) has issued heavy-to-very-heavy rainfall warnings for **20 states**, including Delhi, Punjab, Haryana, Himachal Pradesh, Jammu & Kashmir, and Uttarakhand.
The **Northeast** — Assam, Meghalaya, Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur, Mizoram, Tripura — plus Bihar, Chhattisgarh, Odisha and West Bengal's hills are also under warning.
School and local-body closures are decided **state-by-state and even school-by-school** — India has no single national rain-holiday rule.
Coastal Konkan, including **Mumbai, Thane and Palghar**, is bracing for a fresh orange alert from **August 24**, signaling this rain spell isn't the last.

depth.background: India's **monsoon season** (roughly June to September) delivers about **70% of the country's annual rainfall** and underpins agriculture, drinking-water supply, and hydropower generation for over a billion people. The IMD uses a **color-coded alert system** — green (no warning), yellow (be aware), orange (be prepared), red (take action) — to communicate how severe expected weather is to state governments, who then make the actual calls on school closures, transport, and emergency response.

stories.title: Russia hits Kyiv again before dawn, killing one and wounding a 7-year-old girl
stories.what_happened: In the early hours of Saturday, Russian missiles and drones struck central Kyiv, killing one person and wounding six others, including a 7-year-old girl who was among four people hospitalized, according to mayor Vitali Klitschko. A residential building took a direct hit, and the blast wave also damaged the compound of a nearby kindergarten. This is the fourth time in five days that Russia has struck the Ukrainian capital: Thursday's attack alone killed 16 people and injured more than 40 after Russia launched dozens of missiles and 168 drones overnight, of which Ukraine's air force says it intercepted roughly 90%. A separate strike on Saturday in central Kyiv's Shevchenkivskyi district killed three more people. City officials say this is now the most sustained and deadly run of attacks on Kyiv since the war began.
key_points: Russian missiles and drones hit **central Kyiv** before dawn, killing **one person** and wounding **six**, including a **7-year-old girl**.
A **residential building** was hit directly and the blast also damaged a **kindergarten compound**, mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
It is the **fourth major strike on Kyiv in five days** — Thursday's barrage alone killed **16 people** and wounded more than 40.
Kyiv officials describe this run of attacks as the **bloodiest stretch of the war** for the capital since Russia's 2022 invasion began.

depth.background: Russia has spent nearly three and a half years grinding through a war it launched by invading Ukraine in February 2022. Since mid-2025 the front lines have moved slowly, so Russia has leaned harder on long-range **missile and drone strikes** deep inside Ukraine — hitting cities far from the front, including the capital, Kyiv — to pressure the government and wear down civilian morale and infrastructure. Peace talks brokered by outside powers have repeatedly stalled without a ceasefire. This week's cluster of strikes on Kyiv is the most intense since the war's early months.

thread.previously: We reported that Russia's overnight barrage on Kyiv killed a dozen people, part of what officials called the bloodiest stretch of the missile war on Ukraine since the invasion began.
thread.changed: Russia struck Kyiv again before dawn today, a fourth major hit on the capital in five days. This time the toll was smaller — one dead, six wounded — but the pattern of near-daily strikes on the same city is what has officials alarmed.

stories.title: Trade talks with Canada collapse — Trump slaps 50% tariffs on $20 billion of Canadian goods
stories.what_happened: Trade talks between Washington and Ottawa collapsed late Friday night, and the 50% tariffs on Canadian goods that had been threatened — then paused — went into effect at midnight. The duties apply under **Section 338** of the Tariff Act of 1930 and cover about **$20 billion** worth of Canadian exports, including hockey sticks, building materials, liquor, and certain clothing categories. Prime Minister Mark Carney said 'important progress' had been made in the talks but that it 'has not been enough to meet our objectives for Canadians,' and pledged Canada would match the US tariffs dollar for dollar. Because Section 338 has never been used before, legal experts expect Canada or affected US importers to challenge it in court almost immediately.
key_points: Talks broke down late Friday night, triggering **50% tariffs** on roughly **$20 billion** of Canadian goods at the stroke of midnight
Trump invoked **Section 338** of the 1930 Tariff Act — a presidential power that has **never been used before**
The duties hit everyday goods: **hockey sticks, building materials, liquor, and clothing**
Canadian PM **Mark Carney** vowed to **'match those tariffs dollar for dollar'**
The move is expected to be **challenged in court almost immediately**

depth.background: Trump has spent 2026 waging an on-again, off-again tariff war with dozens of trading partners, using emergency economic powers to impose duties without Congress. In **February 2026**, the **Supreme Court struck down** his use of the **IEEPA** (a law meant for genuine national emergencies) to impose country-specific tariffs, ruling it unconstitutional — forcing the White House to hunt for other legal tools. Section 338 is one of those tools: a Depression-era clause that lets a president slap duties of up to 50% on any country found to 'discriminate' against US commerce, and it had literally never been invoked until now. Trump had already paused a threatened 50% Canada tariff once, on **August 18**, after Carney announced what looked like a breakthrough — but that truce didn't hold.

stories.title: India's forex reserves jump $9.9 billion, closing in on the all-time record
stories.what_happened: The RBI's weekly data, released Friday, showed India's forex reserves climbed by **$9.905 billion** in the week ended August 14, bringing the total to **$716.907 billion**. This follows an even bigger jump of **$14.136 billion** the previous week — together, two of the sharpest weekly gains of the year. Despite the rebound, reserves remain below the **all-time high of $728.494 billion** touched in the week ended February 27, just before the Iran war and its oil-price shock began draining India's reserves. Part of the recent rebuild has come through roughly **$56.85 billion** in concessional swap arrangements the government and RBI have used to attract additional foreign-currency inflows.
key_points: India's **foreign exchange reserves** rose **$9.9 billion** in the week ending August 14, to **$716.9 billion**.
That's the **second big weekly jump in a row** — reserves rose $14.1 billion the week before.
Reserves are now closing in on the **all-time record of $728.5 billion**, hit in late February 2026.
The RBI has also pulled in about **$56.85 billion** through concessional currency-swap measures aimed at boosting reserves.
The buildup comes even as the rupee stays under pressure from high oil prices tied to the **Iran/Strait of Hormuz crisis**.

depth.background: A country's foreign exchange (forex) reserves are the stockpile of foreign currencies — mostly US dollars — that its central bank holds. India's central bank, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)**, uses these reserves to pay for imports, defend the rupee when it weakens sharply, and reassure investors the country can meet its foreign obligations. Reserves had been sliding for months as the RBI spent heavily — an estimated **$46 billion** — to smooth the rupee's fall after oil prices spiked following February's outbreak of the Iran war, which disrupted the Strait of Hormuz that carries a large share of India's crude and gas imports.

stories.title: Blackstone pitches a $36 billion loan to keep Anthropic's AI chips running
stories.what_happened: **Blackstone**, the world's largest alternative-asset manager, has begun sounding out investors about arranging a roughly **$36 billion debt package** to help Anthropic pay for the Google-made AI chips (TPUs) it depends on to run its models. Banks are reportedly already lining up investor meetings for the financing. This would mark Anthropic's **second large debt financing tied specifically to chip consumption**, following a similar structure used earlier this year. The debt talks are happening in parallel with Anthropic's push toward an **IPO it is targeting for as early as October 2026**, with bankers pricing the company's potential market value as high as **$2 trillion** on its first day of trading. Anthropic's losses ballooned to nearly **$42 billion in 2025**, underscoring just how much cash the company burns to stay competitive with rivals like OpenAI.
key_points: Blackstone is in early talks to arrange roughly **$36 billion** in debt for Anthropic's AI computing buildout.
The money would fund the **Google chips** (TPUs) Anthropic rents to train and run its Claude models.
It would be Anthropic's **second major debt deal** this year, on top of billions already raised in equity.
The news lands as Anthropic preps a blockbuster **IPO as early as October**, at a valuation investors are pricing near **$2 trillion**.
Anthropic's 2025 net losses hit nearly **$42 billion** — a five-fold jump from 2024 — showing how costly the AI arms race has become.

depth.background: Training and running large AI models like Anthropic's Claude requires enormous amounts of specialized computing power — mostly rented from cloud providers like Google and Amazon rather than owned outright. That rented compute is expensive enough that AI labs increasingly borrow money (debt) to pay for it, instead of only relying on investors buying equity (ownership stakes). Anthropic has already raised **tens of billions** from investors, including a $65 billion round earlier this year, but its cash burn has kept pace with its growth. Wall Street banks — Morgan Stanley, Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan — are also working on Anthropic's IPO in parallel, meaning the company is trying to lock in both debt and public-market capital at the same time.

stories.title: Championship leader Antonelli damages his floor in a Zandvoort gravel excursion, costing him a shot at pole
stories.what_happened: During **Sprint Qualifying** at Zandvoort on Friday, championship leader **Kimi Antonelli** ran wide at the penultimate corner on his opening lap in SQ1, sending his Mercedes through the gravel. The excursion punched **holes in the car's floor**, which the team estimated cost roughly **25 points of downforce**. Still carrying the damage into the rest of the session, Antonelli could only qualify **5th**, 0.227 seconds behind teammate **George Russell**, who claimed pole. Antonelli said afterward it was hard to **rebuild confidence** in the car, especially through slow-speed sections, even after mechanics patched the floor — though he said the gap back to the front was "decently close" and he'd have another shot in Saturday's sprint race and main qualifying.
key_points: **Kimi Antonelli**, currently leading the F1 drivers' championship, ran wide at the **penultimate corner** on his first lap of Sprint Qualifying at Zandvoort.
The excursion left his Mercedes with **holes in the floor**, which the team initially estimated cost around **25 points of downforce**.
He could only manage **5th place** in Sprint Qualifying, **0.227 seconds** behind teammate **George Russell**, who took pole.
Antonelli admitted a **confidence knock** afterward, saying he struggled in low-speed corners even once repairs were made.
Mercedes team principal **Toto Wolff** confirmed the car was genuinely damaged, not just a driving-mistake excuse.

depth.background: **Kimi Antonelli**, Mercedes' young Italian driver, has emerged as the surprise **championship leader** in the 2026 F1 season, putting him under the spotlight at every race weekend. A **floor** is the flat underside of an F1 car that generates most of its downforce (the aerodynamic force pushing the car onto the track for grip); damage there — like holes from scraping over gravel or kerbs — can badly hurt a car's handling, especially in slow corners where the floor's airflow matters most.

stories.title: Sensex, Nifty end a volatile session almost flat as crude and bond-yield stress cap the rally
stories.what_happened: Indian markets opened higher on Friday, extending Thursday's bounce, with the Sensex briefly up over 160 points and the Nifty near 24,300. But the gains evaporated through the day, and both indices closed almost exactly where they started: the **Sensex finished up just 3.11 points at 77,540.83**, and the **Nifty rose 20.15 points to 24,252.00** — both essentially flat. Sector performance was split: metal, realty and select pharma names attracted buying, while IT, FMCG, auto and media stocks weighed the index down. The muted session came as **Brent crude neared $94 a barrel** and global bond yields kept climbing, both of which make investors more cautious about holding riskier equities.
key_points: Sensex closed up just **3.11 points at 77,540.83**; Nifty rose **20.15 points to 24,252.00** — essentially unchanged.
The session was **rangebound and volatile**, giving back most of the morning's opening gains.
**Brent crude oil** approaching **$94 a barrel** and rising US bond yields kept investors cautious.
**Metal and realty stocks** gained while **IT, FMCG, auto, media and pharma** shares dragged the index down.
It follows Thursday's rally that snapped a **seven-session losing streak** — today's flat close shows that bounce has stalled.

depth.background: Indian equity benchmarks had been sliding for seven straight sessions before Thursday's rebound, hit by a mix of global bond-market stress, elevated crude oil prices, and Middle East tensions tied to the US-Iran standoff. Thursday's rally — Nifty up 0.64%, Sensex up 0.82% — offered relief, but analysts had already flagged that follow-through buying looked fragile given how many global headwinds remained unresolved. Global bond yields have been climbing worldwide this week, which makes borrowing more expensive everywhere and tends to pull money out of riskier assets like emerging-market stocks including India's.

thread.previously: We reported that the Sensex and Nifty snapped a seven-session losing streak on Thursday as global bond-market jitters eased, with the Nifty up 0.64% and Sensex up 0.82%.
thread.changed: Friday's follow-through fizzled: both indices closed almost exactly flat as Brent crude neared $94 and bond yields kept climbing, showing the rebound hasn't yet turned into a sustained recovery.

stories.title: Yemen edges toward all-out war as Houthi attacks trigger the bloodiest clashes since the 2022 truce
stories.what_happened: On August 6, Houthi forces launched a wave of missile and drone strikes on Yemeni government military camps in Hadramout and Marib provinces, killing at least **30 soldiers** and wounding 15 more — one of the deadliest single attacks since the 2022 truce. A military source told AFP the toll may have reached **58 dead**; the Houthis claim to have killed or wounded 'hundreds,' though that figure is unverified. Fighting has since spread across multiple fronts — Taiz, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, al-Dhale and Lahj — with the government reporting it carried out more than **100 military operations** against Houthi positions in a single 24-hour stretch, using drones, artillery and rocket launchers. On Friday, UN special envoy **Hans Grundberg** told the UN Security Council that Yemen faces its highest risk of returning to full-scale civil war since the 2022 truce took hold. The truce itself was never formally renewed after it lapsed in October 2022, but had mostly held on the ground until this month's escalation.
key_points: Houthi forces launched their biggest offensive since the 2022 truce, killing at least **30 government soldiers** and wounding dozens in strikes on Hadramout and Marib on **August 6**.
Government sources say the real toll from that first wave may have reached **58 dead**; the Houthis claim they killed or wounded 'hundreds,' unverified.
Fighting has since spread to **Taiz, al-Jawf, Hodeidah, al-Dhale and Lahj**, with Yemeni forces claiming **100+ retaliatory strikes in a single 24-hour period**.
UN special envoy **Hans Grundberg** told the Security Council Yemen faces its **highest risk of all-out war since the 2022 truce**.
The truce that has held, imperfectly, since **April 2022** paused eight years of civil war between the Iran-backed Houthis and the internationally recognized government.

depth.background: Yemen's civil war began in 2014 when the Houthi movement, an armed group backed by **Iran**, seized the capital Sanaa and much of the country's north, pushing the internationally recognized government into exile in the south. A Saudi-led coalition intervened to back the government, and the war killed hundreds of thousands of people and triggered one of the world's worst humanitarian crises before a **UN-brokered truce in April 2022** mostly paused the front-line fighting, even though it was never formally renewed. Since then, sporadic clashes have continued, but what's happening now is different in scale: since **August 6**, Houthi attacks have killed dozens of government soldiers in a single push, and the government has responded with over a hundred strikes of its own.

stories.title: Championship leader Antonelli confirms he'll take his engine penalty at his home Italian GP in Monza
stories.what_happened: Antonelli confirmed he will take a power-unit-related grid penalty at the **Italian Grand Prix in Monza on September 6** — his own home race, in front of Italian fans — after Mercedes decided it was the best track on the calendar to absorb the hit. He's already used three power-unit allocations this season, including one taken at Spa-Francorchamps just before the summer break, and this will be his fourth. Mercedes' reasoning: Monza's long straights and light-downforce layout make it one of the **easiest circuits in F1 to overtake on**, so starting from further back costs Antonelli less time than it would at a tighter track. Antonelli said that although it's disappointing to take the penalty at his home race, protecting his 50-point championship lead over Lewis Hamilton matters more to him right now. Mercedes' overall reliability troubles mean teammate George Russell is also expected to take a similar grid penalty before the season concludes.
key_points: **Kimi Antonelli**, F1's 2026 title leader with a **50-point cushion** over Lewis Hamilton, will take a **grid penalty at Monza** on September 6.
It's his **fourth and final power-unit allocation** for the season after taking a new one at Spa before the summer break.
Mercedes chose Monza — his **home race** — because it's **one of the easiest F1 tracks to overtake on**, making recovery from the back easier.
Antonelli: **'right now I'm thinking more about the championship'** than protecting a clean home Grand Prix.
Teammate **George Russell** also faces a likely grid drop before the season ends, per Mercedes' broader reliability picture.

depth.background: In Formula 1, each car is allowed a limited number of power-unit components (engine, turbo, energy store, etc.) per season before drivers start incurring automatic **grid penalties** for using extra ones — a rule designed to control costs and engine-development spending. Antonelli, an 18-year-old Italian in his second full F1 season with Mercedes, has led the drivers' championship for much of 2026, but Mercedes' power unit has needed more replacements than rivals', forcing a strategic call on **where** to absorb the inevitable penalty rather than **whether** to take one at all.

thread.previously: Yesterday we reported Mercedes was bringing a big upgrade to Zandvoort, but that engine-related grid penalties looked 'almost inevitable' for both Antonelli and Russell before the season ends.
thread.changed: Today Antonelli confirmed exactly where he'll take that hit: his home Italian Grand Prix at Monza on September 6, prioritising the title fight over a clean home race.

stories.title: Russia says it's open to 'new ideas' on ending the Ukraine war — but only ones that fit Putin's terms
stories.what_happened: Speaking on Thursday, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Sergey Ryabkov said Moscow is willing to hear 'new ideas' for ending the war, but stressed any proposal must align with **President Vladimir Putin's** own goals and the 'realities on the ground' — meaning battlefield gains Russia already holds. The remarks come as the Kremlin says it currently has no update on when US mediators Kushner and Witkoff, who led earlier negotiations, might return to the table. Ukraine, for its part, is still awaiting the mediators' return and has repeated it will not unilaterally pull troops from the **Donbas**, insisting any territorial discussion happen based on the current line of contact rather than Russia's maximalist claims. The statement reads publicly conciliatory but changes nothing about the substance of Russia's position.
key_points: Russia's Deputy Foreign Minister **Sergey Ryabkov** said Moscow will consider 'new ideas' to end the war, but only if they match **'realities on the ground'** — diplomatic code for Russia's own terms.
The Kremlin says it has **no new information** on a return visit by US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who led earlier rounds of talks.
The two core sticking points are unchanged: Russia wants **all of the Donbas region** ceded, while Ukraine refuses to withdraw troops unilaterally.
This is the latest twist in over a year of on-again, off-again truce attempts, including short-lived ceasefires earlier in 2026 that both collapsed within weeks.

depth.background: Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in **February 2022**. Since then, repeated rounds of US-brokered talks — including a push earlier this year involving envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff — have produced brief truces but no lasting peace, largely because Moscow and Kyiv want fundamentally different things from any deal. **Territory and security guarantees** remain the two issues neither side will bend on: Russia wants Ukraine to formally cede the Donbas region it has only partly captured by force, while Ukraine says it won't hand over land it still controls without a fight at the negotiating table.

stories.title: Fed Chair Powell all but promises a September rate cut, sending stocks and gold to fresh highs
stories.what_happened: Federal Reserve Chair **Jerome Powell** delivered his keynote speech at the Jackson Hole symposium on Friday, saying the 'baseline outlook and the shifting balance of risks may warrant adjusting our policy stance' — widely read as a strong signal the Fed will cut its benchmark interest rate at its September meeting. He acknowledged inflation risks remain 'tilted to the upside' as tariff-related price pressures become 'clearly visible,' but said he was increasingly worried about a weakening job market. Markets reacted immediately: the **Dow Jones** jumped **800 points (1.9%)** to a fresh record, the **S&P 500** rose about 1.5%, and the **Nasdaq** gained 1.9%, led by gains in Nvidia, Tesla, Meta and Broadcom. Gold rose 1.1% to **$3,419 an ounce** and Bitcoin climbed 2.7%, while the dollar weakened. Interest-rate traders raised their odds of a September rate cut from about 70% in the morning to **over 91%** by the end of the day.
key_points: Powell said the economic outlook '**may warrant adjusting**' the Fed's policy stance — market-speak for a rate cut is coming.
Traders' odds of a **September rate cut** jumped from **70% to over 91%** within hours of the speech.
The **Dow rose 800 points (1.9%)** to a record close; the Nasdaq gained **1.9%**; gold rose to **$3,419/oz**.
Powell flagged **two-sided risk** — a cooling job market alongside inflation that's still '**tilted to the upside**' from tariffs.
The US dollar weakened on the news, a classic signal that traders expect **cheaper borrowing** ahead.

depth.background: The Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium is an annual gathering of the world's top central bankers in Wyoming, and the Federal Reserve Chair's speech there is one of the most closely watched events on the global economic calendar because it often previews the Fed's next move. Coming into this year's speech, investors were split on whether the Fed would cut interest rates at its **September meeting**, given a US economy showing both a cooling labor market and inflation that remains above the Fed's **2% target**, partly due to import tariffs. Interest rates are the tool the Fed uses to speed up or slow down the economy: cutting them makes borrowing cheaper, which usually boosts stocks and growth but can also fuel inflation.

stories.title: Verstappen tops final practice at his emotional last home race, as Zandvoort bows out of F1
stories.what_happened: Formula 1 returned from its summer break on Friday for the only practice session of Zandvoort's **sprint weekend**, and **Max Verstappen** set the pace with a lap of **1 minute 11.852 seconds**. He beat Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin by **0.278 seconds**, with Lewis Hamilton's Ferrari third and Verstappen's Red Bull teammate Sergio Perez fourth. Verstappen topped the times on **all three available tyre compounds**, suggesting his pace advantage wasn't just a one-lap sprint-fuel trick. The session was red-flagged once, after Sauber's Nico Hulkenberg spun into the gravel trap at the penultimate corner. Because this is a sprint weekend format, this single practice hour was the **only** chance teams had to fine-tune their setups before **sprint qualifying** later Friday and the **Grand Prix on Sunday**. It's also billed as Verstappen's **emotional final home race** at Zandvoort, since the track is dropping off the F1 calendar after this event.
key_points: **Max Verstappen** set the fastest time in Friday's only practice session at Zandvoort, **1:11.852**, on what is his **last home Dutch Grand Prix**.
He finished **0.278 seconds** ahead of Aston Martin's **Fernando Alonso**, with Ferrari's **Lewis Hamilton** third and Red Bull teammate **Sergio Perez** fourth.
Verstappen was **fastest on all three tyre compounds**, a strong early signal for the rest of the weekend.
A **red flag** interrupted the session after Nico Hulkenberg spun into the gravel at the second-to-last corner.
This is **Zandvoort's final Formula 1 race** after returning to the calendar in 2021 — and it's also a **sprint weekend**, so this was the only practice session all weekend.

depth.background: Zandvoort, the seaside circuit near Amsterdam, returned to the F1 calendar in 2021 after a **36-year absence**, largely because of the huge home following Max Verstappen built after joining Red Bull. This weekend marks the track's **farewell F1 race** — it won't return to the calendar after this. Verstappen has become something of a local phenomenon here, with the stands turning into a sea of orange ("Oranje") every year he races at Zandvoort, and he's won here multiple times since the track's return. Because this is a **sprint race weekend**, teams only get this one practice session to set up their cars before qualifying and the sprint race take over — raising the stakes on every lap.

stories.title: New York overtakes Silicon Valley in raw tech headcount for the first time in 13 years
stories.what_happened: CBRE's latest annual tech-talent report finds that the New York metro area now employs 394,300 tech workers, narrowly surpassing the San Francisco Bay Area's 375,730 — the first time New York has taken the lead in the study's 13-year history. The shift reflects diverging trends over 2022–2025: the Bay Area's tech workforce fell 6% amid waves of layoffs at major tech companies, while New York's grew more than 8%. A big driver is New York's finance sector, which has been aggressively hiring tech and AI talent directly into banks and asset managers rather than pure tech firms. Even so, when CBRE weighs a broader set of 13 factors — including wages, talent concentration, rents, and the supply of new graduates — the Bay Area still ranks first overall, followed by Seattle, Toronto, New York, Austin, and Washington DC. Separately, workers with AI-specific skills across the US and Canada grew 45% year-over-year to about 751,000 by mid-2026, with both San Francisco and New York each adding more than 20,000 AI-specific jobs since mid-2025.
key_points: New York's metro area now counts **394,300 tech workers**, edging past the San Francisco Bay Area's **375,730** — the first time that's happened in **13 years** of this industry tracking.
From **2022 to 2025**, the Bay Area's tech workforce **shrank 6%** while New York's **grew more than 8%**, per real-estate firm CBRE.
The shift is driven largely by **Wall Street hiring AI and tech talent directly** into finance roles, even as pure tech companies kept cutting jobs in the Bay Area.
Despite losing the headcount lead, the Bay Area still ranks **first overall** on CBRE's broader scorecard, which also weighs wage levels, talent depth and graduate supply.

depth.background: For as long as the modern tech industry has existed, the San Francisco Bay Area — Silicon Valley plus San Francisco itself — has been synonymous with the biggest concentration of tech workers in the US. Real-estate firm **CBRE** has tracked this 'tech talent' competition across US metro areas for 13 years using a scorecard of factors like headcount, wages, and graduate pipelines. New York has long been a strong second city for tech, but has never actually had more tech workers than the Bay Area — until now.

stories.title: Rahul Gandhi sits on a police-station dharna over a pellet-gun victim — and Delhi Police agrees to file an FIR
stories.what_happened: On Thursday, Rahul Gandhi visited two Delhi police stations with Sahil Lochab, demanding an FIR be registered over the pellet-gun injuries Lochab suffered on July 20. After a meeting with Deputy Commissioner of Police (Central) Sachin Sharma failed to produce a commitment, Gandhi and Lochab sat down in a dharna (sit-in protest) outside the Parliament Street police station. Police told them the refusal to register an FIR came on **'orders from the top,'** implying political pressure from above. Priyanka Gandhi, Salman Khurshid, Randeep Singh Surjewala, and other senior Congress figures joined the protest. Union Minister **JP Nadda** criticized the demonstration as **'cheap, attention-seeking politics.'** Following the standoff, Delhi Police agreed to register the FIR.
key_points: Gandhi protested with **Sahil Lochab**, a 19-year-old allegedly hit by police pellets during a **July 20 Jantar Mantar student protest**.
An **AIIMS medical report** reportedly found over **200 shells lodged in his body**, including **3 in one eye**, costing him his vision there.
Police initially refused to register an FIR, telling Gandhi they had **'orders from the top.'**
Priyanka Gandhi and senior Congress leaders **joined the sit-in** after talks with a police officer failed.
Delhi Police later **agreed to register the FIR** after the standoff drew national attention.

depth.background: An FIR (First Information Report) is the formal document Indian police must file to officially open a criminal investigation — without one, a complaint effectively goes nowhere. Sahil Lochab was injured on July 20 during a student protest at Delhi's Jantar Mantar/Connaught Place, allegedly hit by pellets fired by police, and was treated first at Lady Hardinge Hospital before being referred to AIIMS, India's top public hospital. Rahul Gandhi, the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha (India's lower house of Parliament), has repeatedly used direct, visible protests like this to pressure the government on issues of alleged state overreach.

stories.title: India's factories slow to a 5-year low even as services rebound, flash PMI shows
stories.what_happened: HSBC's Flash India Composite PMI, compiled by S&P Global, rose to **54.6** in August from a final July reading of 54.3 — July's number had been India's weakest in over four years. The improvement was driven entirely by services, whose sub-index rose to 54.5 from 53.3, while the Manufacturing PMI actually fell, to 52.9 from 53.5 in July — its softest expansion in five years. Survey respondents pointed to weaker export order growth in factories even as domestic services demand held up.
key_points: The **Composite Flash PMI rose to 54.6** in August, up slightly from July's over-**4-year low** of 54.3
**Manufacturing PMI fell to 52.9**, its weakest expansion pace in **five years**
**Services PMI climbed to 54.5**, driving the overall improvement
Any reading **above 50 still means growth** — India's private sector is expanding, just more slowly on the factory side

depth.background: The **Flash PMI** is a monthly survey of purchasing managers at hundreds of companies, asking whether new orders, output, and hiring are rising or falling — a reading **above 50 means expansion**, **below 50 means contraction**. It's one of the fastest, most-watched early readings on how an economy is actually doing, weeks before official GDP data arrives. India's composite reading had slumped to a **52-month low** in July, so August's tick-up is a mild relief, but the manufacturing side alone is now growing at its slowest pace in **five years** even as services carry the overall number higher.

stories.title: ED raids revive an 8-year-old ₹113-crore crypto scam, traces alleged kingpin to Dubai
stories.what_happened: The ED's Mumbai Zonal Office carried out search operations across multiple properties in Mumbai and Thane connected to the MTC cryptocurrency investment scheme, seizing roughly ₹1 crore in cash along with incriminating documents and digital devices. Investigators allege investors were cheated of about ₹113 crore after the scheme's operators manipulated the value of the MTC coin across several linked platforms to attract and retain buyers. The agency named Amit Madanlal Lakhanpal as the alleged mastermind; he and some associates are accused of leaving India after obtaining Antigua and Barbuda passports through a citizenship-by-investment program and are now believed to be living in Dubai under assumed identities. The ED also summoned Taha Hafiz Qazi, described as technical support staff, and chief accountant Sachin Vasant Shelar for questioning. The agency is expected to seek Interpol's help if it confirms Lakhanpal remains in Dubai.
key_points: India's **Enforcement Directorate** searched properties in **Mumbai and Thane** tied to the **MTC (Money Trade Coin)** cryptocurrency scheme, seizing about **₹1 crore in cash**.
Investors were allegedly cheated of around **₹113 crore** through a scheme that manipulated the value of its own coin to lure and retain buyers.
The alleged mastermind, **Amit Madanlal Lakhanpal**, is accused of fleeing to **Dubai** on an **Antigua and Barbuda passport** obtained through a citizenship-by-investment scheme.
The case had **languished for nearly a decade** in local Thane police files before this ED action — its first serious central-agency move.

depth.background: India's Enforcement Directorate (ED) is the federal agency that investigates financial crimes like money laundering, and it often steps into cases that started as local police complaints once cross-border money trails emerge. The MTC scheme is an old one: it dates back roughly eight years, when it promised investors returns from a cryptocurrency called Money Trade Coin. Complaints piled up with Thane City Police, but the case saw little central-agency movement for years — a common pattern in India's early-generation crypto fraud cases, many of which pre-date the country's current crypto regulations.

stories.title: Sri Lanka names uncapped duo Mishara and Arachchige to plug its injury-hit batting for the Colombo Test
stories.what_happened: Sri Lanka Cricket announced its squad for the second Test against India, confirming **Kamil Mishara** and **Sahan Arachchige** — both uncapped at Test level — as direct replacements for the injured senior batters, alongside a squad that includes **four fast bowlers**. The selection confirms Sri Lanka will go into the Colombo Test with a batting order stripped of experience: no Mendis, no Chandimal, no Nissanka. Head coach Gary Kirsten's side will lean on the uncapped duo's recent domestic form as India, already 1-0 up after the Galle Test, look to close out the series.
key_points: Sri Lanka named its squad for the **2nd Test vs India** in Colombo, drafting in **uncapped batters Kamil Mishara and Sahan Arachchige**.
Both were picked on the back of **strong recent domestic form**, the stated reason for their inclusion.
The squad carries **four pacers**, a notably pace-heavy attack for a subcontinental Test.
The changes follow the injury exodus reported after Galle: **Kusal Mendis** (hamstring), **Dinesh Chandimal** (concussion protocol) and **Pathum Nissanka** (wrist recovery) are all unavailable.
Sri Lanka trails the two-Test series **1-0** after a **165-run defeat** in Galle, and now fields a batting order with almost no senior experience against India's in-form attack.

depth.background: India beat Sri Lanka by **165 runs** in the first Test in Galle, and Sri Lanka's top order — already thin on depth — lost three senior batters to injury in the space of a week: Mendis to a hamstring picked up in the **Lanka Premier League**, Chandimal to a first-Test concussion that triggers a mandatory **7-day stand-down**, and Nissanka to a lingering wrist injury. Coach **Gary Kirsten** has been trying to rebuild Sri Lanka's Test depth, and this squad announcement is the team's answer to that injury crisis ahead of the second Test starting **August 23** at Colombo's SSC ground.

thread.previously: We reported that Sri Lanka would head into the second Test against India missing three senior batters — Kusal Mendis (hamstring), Dinesh Chandimal (concussion protocol) and likely Pathum Nissanka (wrist recovery) — and flagged the team announcement as the thing to watch for.
thread.changed: Sri Lanka has now named its actual replacement squad: uncapped batters Kamil Mishara and Sahan Arachchige have been drafted in, with the squad also carrying four pacers, resolving who steps into the vacated batting slots.

stories.title: RBI's deputy governor says India's growth may beat forecasts and near 7%
stories.what_happened: Speaking at an event hosted by the Madras School of Economics in Chennai, RBI Deputy Governor Poonam Gupta said India's economic growth for the financial year ending March could come in close to **7%**, beating the central bank's official **6.7% forecast**. She attributed the upbeat outlook to an expected strong April–June quarter, with official growth figures for that quarter due to be released later this month. She added: **'Going forward, notwithstanding these shocks, I would say, 7.5 per cent is a given and we should aspire to do better than that.'** Her comments come even as she acknowledged the economy faces real headwinds, including an inadequate monsoon and elevated energy costs.
key_points: **Poonam Gupta**, RBI Deputy Governor, said growth could come in near **7%**, above the RBI's own **6.7% forecast**.
Her optimism rests on an expected **strong April–June quarter**, with official data due later this month.
Economists' estimates for the quarter range widely, from **6.9% to 8%**.
Gupta said India should ultimately **'aspire' to 7.5%-plus** annual growth over time.
This comes despite headwinds like a **patchy monsoon** and **elevated energy costs**.

depth.background: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is India's central bank, and its Monetary Policy Committee sets interest rates partly based on how fast the economy is growing — faster growth with high inflation typically argues for holding or raising rates, while slower growth argues for cuts. GDP (Gross Domestic Product) growth is the broadest measure of how much an economy's output of goods and services expanded over a period, usually a year or a quarter. India has been one of the world's fastest-growing major economies, and the RBI's own forecasts are watched closely as a baseline that markets, businesses, and the government plan around.

stories.title: Israeli settlers and troops kill two Palestinians, including a teenager, in separate West Bank shootings
stories.what_happened: On Friday, a confrontation broke out in the West Bank town of **Sa'ir** after Palestinians threw stones at a group of Israelis who had entered the area without official authorization. Israeli soldiers were dispatched to the scene; in the chaos, a security official opened fire, and a **17-year-old Palestinian, Karim Sanad Raja Shalaldeh, was killed**, with another man wounded. The teen's father said at the hospital that it was **settlers who killed his son**, not soldiers — a distinction Israeli authorities have not fully clarified. In a **separate incident** the same day elsewhere in the West Bank, Israeli forces killed another Palestinian, bringing the day's West Bank death toll to two.
key_points: A **17-year-old Palestinian**, named locally as Karim Sanad Raja Shalaldeh, was shot dead in the town of **Sa'ir**, north of Hebron, after Palestinians threw stones at Israelis present in the area.
A **second Palestinian was killed** the same day in a separate shooting involving Israeli forces elsewhere in the West Bank, according to wire reports.

The Israeli military said soldiers were sent to Sa'ir after Palestinians threw rocks at **Israeli civilians who were there without prior authorization**; some Israelis were hurt before a security official opened fire.
The teenager's father told the Associated Press at the hospital that it was **settlers, not soldiers**, who killed his son.
The killings add to a documented **rise in settler violence** across the West Bank that rights monitors and the UN have tracked through 2026.

depth.background: The **West Bank** is Palestinian territory that Israel has militarily occupied since 1967; roughly 500,000 **Israeli settlers** now live there in communities most of the world considers illegal under international law, alongside about 3 million Palestinians. Settler violence against Palestinians — attacks on people, homes, and farmland — has escalated sharply since the Gaza war began in 2023, often with **little accountability** from Israeli authorities, according to human-rights groups. Sa'ir, near Hebron, sits in an area with a long history of friction between Palestinian residents and nearby settlements.

stories.title: Supreme Court cuts the mandatory law-practice rule for judge candidates from 3 years to 1, adds a year of training
stories.what_happened: The Supreme Court, in a verdict pronounced by **Chief Justice Surya Kant's bench** at **10:30 AM** on August 21, modified its own May 2025 ruling: instead of requiring 3 years of prior legal practice to sit the Civil Judge (Junior Division) exam, candidates now need just **1 year of practice**. The court added new requirements on the back end — successful candidates must complete **1 year of training at a judicial academy**, followed by **1 year of structured clerkship under a sitting judge**, before being confirmed as judicial officers, and will be paid half a magistrate's salary during that period. The court also carved out relief for graduates caught in limbo since its original ruling: anyone who graduated law school between **May 20, 2025 and March 31, 2027** can sit the exam with no prior practice requirement at all, but if selected, will be appointed only as a 'trainee judicial officer' and must still complete the training and clerkship. The bench separately heard a plea to relax the requirement for candidates with disabilities.
key_points: The court refused to scrap the practice requirement entirely but **cut it from 3 years to 1 year** of legal practice before candidates can sit the Civil Judge exam
Selected candidates must now also complete **1 year of judicial academy training** plus **1 year of supervised clerkship** before taking the bench
Trainees will be paid **half the salary** of a sitting Judicial Magistrate First Class during this training period
Law graduates from **May 2025 to March 2027** get a one-time waiver — they can sit the exam with **zero practice years**, but must still do the training and clerkship
The bench was led by **Chief Justice Surya Kant**, alongside Justices August George Masih and K Vinod Chandran

depth.background: In **May 2025**, the Supreme Court restored a rule requiring **3 years of legal practice** before law graduates could sit the entry-level exam to become a **Civil Judge (Junior Division)** — reversing years of letting fresh graduates apply directly. Petitioners, including bar associations and law students, argued the 3-year rule pushed talented graduates away from judicial careers by forcing years of often-unpaid junior lawyering first, at a time many state judiciaries face **judge shortages**. The court took the rare step of agreeing to review its own decision through review petitions, and today delivered its final word.

stories.title: Gold and silver platform Augmont Enterprises opens its ₹825-crore IPO today
stories.what_happened: Augmont Enterprises Limited's IPO opened for public subscription today, August 21, and will close on August 25. The company is offering shares in a price band of **₹750 to ₹788**, aiming to raise up to **₹825 crore** through the main-board listing on the NSE and BSE. Ahead of the public opening, the company's anchor book — the portion sold to large institutional investors a day before the retail opening — was **oversubscribed, raising ₹246 crore**. The minimum retail investment works out to roughly ₹14,972 for a lot of 19 shares at the upper price band. Nuvama Wealth Management is the lead book-running manager, with listing tentatively expected around August 31.
key_points: Augmont's IPO opens today with a price band of **₹750–₹788 per share**
The issue aims to raise up to **₹825 crore**, closing August 25
Anchor investors have already committed **₹246 crore** ahead of the public opening
Augmont is an **integrated gold and silver platform** serving businesses and retail buyers across India
The listing lands in the middle of a **hot IPO season** already covered by Tempsens and Lalithaa Jewellery's oversubscribed issues

depth.background: An **Initial Public Offering (IPO)** is when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money and get listed on a stock exchange. Before the public opening, companies typically sell a chunk of shares to large institutional **anchor investors** at a fixed price — strong anchor demand is often read as a vote of confidence that helps set the tone for retail investors. Augmont Enterprises, incorporated in 2012, runs an integrated **gold and silver platform** — effectively infrastructure connecting bullion supply, storage, and digital gold/silver products for businesses and consumers, in a country where gold buying is a deep cultural and financial habit.

stories.title: Zomato founder Deepinder Goyal's brain-tracking wearable 'Temple' eyes a $500 million valuation
stories.what_happened: Reports this week say Temple is in talks for a new funding round that would value the company at **$500 million** — more than **2.5 times** its valuation just six months ago. The jump is partly validated by an internal **ESOP buyback** (where the company buys back employee stock options, effectively setting a price for the shares) that already pegged Temple's worth at **$375 million**. Temple's flagship product is an AI-powered wearable priced at roughly **₹80,000** that tracks cerebral blood flow and other brain-related signals, positioning it as a more advanced alternative to wrist-worn fitness trackers. The device is expected to launch commercially by the **end of 2026**.
key_points: **Temple**, the AI health-wearable startup from Zomato/Eternal founder **Deepinder Goyal**, is in a funding round targeting a **$500 million valuation**.
That's up sharply from the **$190 million valuation** it raised at just **six months ago**, in February.
An employee **ESOP buyback** already priced the company at **$375 million**, nearly double the February mark.
Temple's device, priced around **₹80,000**, is worn near the temples to track **cerebral blood flow** and brain activity — not just wrist-based fitness signals.
Backers include marquee investors **Peak XV Partners, Steadview Capital, Vy Capital**, and **Info Edge**.

depth.background: Deepinder Goyal co-founded **Zomato** (now renamed Eternal), one of India's best-known food-delivery and quick-commerce companies, and became one of the country's youngest billionaires after its 2021 IPO. Rather than staying purely in food delivery, Goyal has increasingly bet on new ventures — Temple is his push into **health tech**, wagering that a device worn near the temples can capture richer physiological data (like blood flow to the brain) than the wrist-based sensors used by smartwatches and fitness rings. The company raised **$54 million in seed funding in February 2026** at a $190 million valuation from a strong roster of India-focused investors.

stories.title: BCCI to decide Ajit Agarkar's own future as chief selector — with VVS Laxman floated as a replacement
stories.what_happened: The BCCI is set to meet chief selector Ajit Agarkar after the ongoing Sri Lanka series concludes to discuss extending his contract by one more year, as his current three-year term expires this September. The renewal talks arrive amid friction over Rohit Sharma's ODI future: selectors had reportedly told Rohit directly they planned to move on from him once England's white-ball series wrapped up, while BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia publicly told a different story, saying Rohit **'will continue to represent the country as long as he is in the scheme of things.'** That mixed messaging has reportedly left selectors frustrated with the board's own secretary. Reports also suggest former India great **VVS Laxman** could be considered for the role if the BCCI opts not to continue with Agarkar.
key_points: The BCCI will meet **Ajit Agarkar** after the Sri Lanka series to discuss a **1-year contract extension**.
Agarkar completes **3 years** as selection chairman this September, the maximum before requiring renewal.
The talks are complicated by **tension over Rohit Sharma's ODI future** between selectors and the board.
Selectors reportedly told Rohit privately they'd **move on from him**, while the board's line to media said otherwise.
**VVS Laxman** is reportedly a name under consideration if the board decides against continuing with Agarkar.

depth.background: Ajit Agarkar, a former India fast bowler, has chaired the Board of Control for Cricket in India's (BCCI) men's selection committee since 2023, a period that included two ICC trophy wins — the 2025 Champions Trophy and the 2026 T20 World Cup. Under BCCI rules, a selection committee chairman serves an initial term and can be renewed for one further year. The renewal talks come at an awkward moment: selectors and the BCCI's own administration have reportedly given conflicting signals to the media about whether veteran batter Rohit Sharma still has a future in the ODI side, exposing a rift between the selection panel and the board's public messaging.

stories.title: Hyderabad hit-and-run: Jana Sena MP's son booked after his Aston Martin kills a 26-year-old woman
stories.what_happened: On August 16, **Bharathi Mukhi**, a 26-year-old employee at a Lifestyle store in Hyderabad's Inorbit Mall, was crossing the road in the Madhapur area when she was allegedly hit by a speeding **Aston Martin**. She suffered severe head injuries and was rushed to Apollo Hospital in Jubilee Hills, where doctors declared her dead on arrival. Police identified the driver as **Sanjush**, the son of Jana Sena's Rajya Sabha MP Lingamaneni Ramesh, and took him into custody the same day, administering drunk-driving and drug tests and sending blood samples for forensic analysis. He has now been booked under **Section 106(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita** (India's newer criminal code, which replaced the colonial-era IPC in 2024), the provision covering death caused by negligence.
key_points: **Bharathi Mukhi (26)**, a Lifestyle store employee, was struck and killed while crossing the road in Hyderabad's **Madhapur** area on August 16.
The Aston Martin was allegedly driven at high speed by **Sanjush**, the son of **Jana Sena Party Rajya Sabha MP Lingamaneni Ramesh**.
He was taken into custody the same day and given **drunk-driving and drug tests**; blood samples went to the Forensic Science Laboratory.
He has now been formally **booked under BNS Section 106(1)** — causing death by negligence.
The case has fed a recurring public debate in India about **luxury cars, speed, and impunity for the politically connected**.

depth.background: Hit-and-run and rash-driving cases involving the children of politicians or the wealthy are a recurring flashpoint in Indian public debate, often reigniting arguments over whether the well-connected face real legal consequences. The **Jana Sena Party**, led by actor-turned-politician Pawan Kalyan, is a coalition partner in Andhra Pradesh's ruling alliance, and **Lingamaneni Ramesh** sits in the **Rajya Sabha** (India's upper house of Parliament) as one of its members.

stories.title: Maharashtra bans sale of loose, unpacked cooking oil — violators face up to 7 years in jail
stories.what_happened: Maharashtra's FDA, led by Commissioner **Tukaram Mundhe**, has ordered a statewide ban on the sale of loose or unpacked edible oil, announced this week. Mundhe said the decision followed inspections that uncovered **adulteration, unauthorised blending, poor labelling, repackaging of old oil, and the use of unsuitable containers** at multiple outlets. Under the order, violators will be prosecuted under **Chapter IX of the Food Safety and Standards Act**, which allows for imprisonment and fines depending on the severity of the offence: unsafe food can draw jail time plus fines up to ₹10 lakh, substandard oil up to ₹5 lakh, misbranded oil up to ₹3 lakh, possession of adulterants up to ₹10 lakh, and operating without a valid licence up to ₹10 lakh. The FDA has warned it will take strict action against violators going forward.
key_points: Maharashtra's **Food and Drug Administration (FDA)** has banned the sale of **loose, unpacked edible oil** across the state
Violators face **imprisonment of up to 7 years** and fines running as high as **₹10 lakh** depending on the offence
FDA Commissioner **Tukaram Mundhe** said inspections found widespread **adulteration**, unauthorised blending, and repackaging of old oil in unsuitable containers
The crackdown will be enforced under **Chapter IX of the Food Safety and Standards Act**, which covers unsafe and substandard food
Separate penalty slabs apply for substandard oil, misbranded oil, possession of adulterants, and selling without a valid licence

depth.background: In much of India, cooking oil is still commonly sold **loose** — ladled out from large containers at local shops rather than sold pre-packaged and sealed — because it's often cheaper than branded, bottled oil. That informality, though, makes it far easier for sellers to **adulterate** oil (mix it with cheaper substances), reuse old or reheated oil, or store it in containers that aren't food-safe, all without a consumer being able to tell just by looking. India's **Food Safety and Standards Authority (FSSAI)** framework, enforced at the state level by bodies like Maharashtra's FDA, is meant to catch exactly this kind of unsafe practice, but enforcement against small, informal sellers has historically been patchy.

stories.title: Liam Lawson called up to partner Verstappen at Red Bull after Hadjar fractures his wrist punching a gym bag
stories.what_happened: Red Bull confirmed that Isack Hadjar will miss the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort after fracturing his wrist while punching a heavy bag during a gym workout in the summer break — the team's official statement did not name the cause, but multiple outlets reported it stemmed from a boxing session. **Liam Lawson**, who Hadjar effectively replaced at the senior team earlier this year, has been called up from Racing Bulls to fill in alongside Max Verstappen for the weekend. To cover Lawson's seat, reserve driver **Yuki Tsunoda** returns to a race seat at Racing Bulls, lining up next to British rookie Arvid Lindblad. Hadjar, who sits eighth in the championship after a strong debut season with the senior team, says he is hopeful of being fit to return by the Italian Grand Prix at Monza, the next race on the calendar.
key_points: Hadjar **fractured his wrist punching a heavy bag** during a gym session in the summer break, not in a racing incident.
**Liam Lawson** — demoted from Red Bull's senior team earlier this year — steps back up to partner Max Verstappen for the Dutch GP.
**Yuki Tsunoda** moves down to Racing Bulls, lining up alongside British rookie **Arvid Lindblad**.
Hadjar says he's **hopeful of returning by the Italian GP at Monza**, the next race after Zandvoort.
The reshuffle happens at Verstappen's **emotional final home race** at Zandvoort before the track drops off the calendar.

depth.background: Red Bull runs two F1 teams — the senior Red Bull Racing squad with Max Verstappen, and the junior Racing Bulls team that develops young drivers. Isack Hadjar was promoted to partner Verstappen at the start of this season after a strong rookie year at Racing Bulls, while **Liam Lawson** — who had briefly held Hadjar's senior-team seat before him — was demoted back to Racing Bulls. That set up an awkward dynamic: the driver who lost the senior seat is now the direct replacement for the driver who took it from him. Yuki Tsunoda, meanwhile, has spent the season as Red Bull's reserve driver after also losing his senior seat earlier in the year.

thread.previously: We reported Hadjar would miss the Dutch GP after injuring his wrist in a boxing session during the summer break, with his F1 seat status still unclear.
thread.changed: Red Bull has now confirmed Liam Lawson — his predecessor at the senior team — will fill in for Hadjar at Zandvoort, while Yuki Tsunoda drops back down to partner rookie Arvid Lindblad at Racing Bulls.

stories.title: McLaren and Red Bull get their Paris court date to challenge Gasly's reinstated Monaco podium
stories.what_happened: The FIA has confirmed that the International Court of Appeal will hear McLaren and Red Bull's joint challenge on Tuesday, August 25, in Paris, over the retroactive reversal of Pierre Gasly's Monaco Grand Prix penalties. The reversal — triggered by the 77cm pit-lane measurement error — promoted Gasly from 7th to 3rd, which in turn demoted Isack Hadjar out of what would have been his first F1 podium, and dropped Oscar Piastri and the two Racing Bulls drivers one position each. McLaren formally lodged its appeal, arguing the decision 'creates a situation in which some competitors are disadvantaged by having acted in accordance with the rules and the Stewards' decisions.' The hearing will be held behind closed doors at FIA headquarters.
key_points: The **FIA International Court of Appeal** will hear the case on **Tuesday, August 25** in Paris.
It stems from a discovery that Monaco's pit-lane speed measurement was **off by 77cm**.
That error voided **Pierre Gasly's two speeding penalties**, retroactively promoting him to **3rd place**.
The reshuffle **stripped Isack Hadjar of his first F1 podium** and demoted Oscar Piastri a position.
**McLaren and Red Bull jointly appealed**, arguing the reversal is unfair to drivers who 'played by the rules.'

depth.background: In Formula 1, pit lanes have a strict speed limit (usually 60-80 km/h) enforced by fixed measurement points on the track; a driver caught speeding gets a time penalty added to their race result. After the Monaco Grand Prix, Alpine successfully argued that the measurement points used to time Pierre Gasly's pit-lane speed were positioned 77 centimeters off from where the rules required, making his original penalties invalid. Stewards agreed and voided the penalties, which retroactively moved Gasly from 7th to 3rd place — reshuffling the final classification and the championship points everyone had already banked from that race.

stories.title: Wall Street braces for new Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's first Jackson Hole speech, three weeks before a rate call
stories.what_happened: The Federal Reserve's Jackson Hole symposium runs **August 27–29**, with new Fed Chair **Kevin Warsh** delivering his first keynote as chair on Friday, **August 28** — just three weeks before the Fed's next rate decision on **September 16**. Market pricing for a September move has shifted: futures now put the odds of a rate increase at roughly **34%**, down sharply after July's jobs report showed the US economy **shed 23,000 jobs** while consumer inflation cooled to **3.4%** year-over-year. A recent Bank of America fund-manager survey found **72%** expect no Fed rate move before November's midterm elections. Warsh has told reporters he intends the speech to 'frame the big questions' about long-term structural issues, not offer near-term guidance — continuing a pattern since May of short statements and press conferences that deliberately avoid tipping the Fed's hand.
key_points: Warsh delivers his **first keynote as Fed Chair** on **August 28** at the Jackson Hole symposium, just three weeks before the **September 16** rate decision
Odds of a September hike have fallen to roughly **34%** after July payrolls showed a loss of **23,000 jobs** and inflation cooled to **3.4%**
**72% of fund managers** now see no Fed rate move before the November midterms, per a recent Bank of America survey
Warsh has told reporters he wants the speech to **'frame the big questions'** rather than signal near-term policy — a break from predecessor Jerome Powell's style
Traders are watching gold and the dollar closely, since any hint of **rate cuts** typically pushes bullion higher and weakens the greenback

depth.background: **Jerome Powell's term as Fed Chair ended in May 2026**, and **Kevin Warsh** — a former Fed governor known for a more hawkish, rules-based approach — took over. The Jackson Hole Economic Symposium, held every August in Wyoming, is where sitting Fed chairs have historically previewed their thinking on interest rates, watched by every trader and central banker in the world. Powell used the platform in past years to signal major pivots; since taking over, Warsh has instead kept his public statements short and deliberately avoided giving markets clear guidance.

stories.title: Punjab shuts down for 7 hours as Sikh groups demand release of 'Bandi Singhs' who've finished their sentences
stories.what_happened: Allied groups under the **Qaumi Insaaf Morcha** banner called and enforced a **statewide bandh (shutdown)** across Punjab on August 21, running from **7 AM to 2 PM**, to press their demand for the release of Sikh prisoners the Morcha says have completed their sentences but remain incarcerated. Schools and colleges across the state stayed closed, shops and factories were asked to shut for the duration, and highways along with bus and other transport services were disrupted. The **SGPC**, the powerful body that manages Sikh religious institutions in Punjab, formally extended its support to the bandh call, lending it significant organizational weight. The call came after tensions escalated on **August 15**, when demonstrators tried to march toward Punjab Governor Gulab Chand Kataria's official residence in Chandigarh to press the same demand, and police used tear gas and water cannons to disperse the crowd after protesters tried to breach security barricades near Lok Bhavan.
key_points: The **Qaumi Insaaf Morcha** called a statewide bandh from **7 AM to 2 PM**, backed by the influential **Shiromani Gurdwara Parbandhak Committee (SGPC)**
The core demand: release **Sikh prisoners ('Bandi Singhs')** the Morcha says have already **completed their sentences** but remain jailed
Schools, colleges, shops, factories, buses and highways across Punjab were shut or disrupted during the bandh window
The protest follows an **August 15** clash near the Chandigarh–Mohali border, where police used **tear gas and water cannons** on demonstrators
Punjab Governor **Gulab Chand Kataria** was the target of the earlier march, which was blocked at barricades near Lok Bhavan

depth.background: '**Bandi Singhs**' refers to a group of Sikh prisoners, some convicted decades ago in cases tied to militancy and violence in Punjab during the 1980s-90s insurgency period, whom Sikh religious and political organizations say have already served sentences equivalent to a life term, yet remain in custody. Their release has been a recurring, emotionally charged demand in Punjab and among Sikh communities globally, periodically flaring into major protests. The **Qaumi Insaaf Morcha** ('National Justice Front') is a coalition of Sikh organizations pushing specifically on this issue, and its campaigns have previously drawn support from mainstream religious bodies like the **SGPC**, which administers Sikh gurdwaras (temples) across Punjab.

stories.title: Trump doubles down on 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz as Iran warns of a 'devastating' response to new sanctions
stories.what_happened: Trump repeated and expanded his claim that the US has **'total control'** over the Strait of Hormuz, saying **'I THINK WE WILL KEEP IT!'** and suggesting the US could formally claim the waterway as its own territory once the war against Iran is 'finished.' He described the ongoing US naval blockade as a **'wall of steel'** that Iran cannot counter. In response, officials on Iran's side, including its paramilitary Revolutionary Guard Corps, warned of a **'devastating'** response if the US presses ahead with the sanctions campaign due to be formally announced **Monday** — the plan Bessent has called the most extensive coordinated sanctions effort ever attempted against a single country. China has already declined to take part.
key_points: Trump says the US has **'total control'** of the Strait of Hormuz and floated **declaring it US territory**
The formal rollout of Bessent's **'toughest sanctions in history'** against Iran is due **Monday**
Iran's side warned of a **'devastating' response** if the new sanctions go ahead
The US-Iran war, which began **February 28, 2026**, has already produced **56 reported vessel-damage incidents** in the strait
China has already refused to join the sanctions push, calling it counter-productive

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and the Arabian Peninsula that roughly **one-fifth of the world's oil** passes through — meaning any disruption there ripples straight into gas prices everywhere. Since a US-Iran war broke out on **February 28, 2026**, Washington has run a naval blockade of Iranian ports and carried out repeated strikes, while pairing the military pressure with an escalating economic campaign Trump has branded **'economic D-Day.'** Treasury Secretary Bessent has said the goal is to **'collapse this regime'** by cutting off Iran's oil and banking channels, with China — the biggest buyer of discounted Iranian crude — seen as the campaign's real test.

thread.previously: China's foreign ministry publicly refused to join the new US sanctions campaign against Iran, calling pressure tactics 'not the solution' and urging a diplomatic resolution instead — a rebuff that came the same day Iran's foreign ministry warned any official enforcing the new US sanctions could face prosecution.
thread.changed: With the formal sanctions rollout due Monday, Trump escalated further — declaring the US has 'total control' of the Strait of Hormuz and floating the idea of declaring it US territory — while Iran's side warned of a 'devastating' response if Washington follows through.
