stories.title: Jordan Cox's Test chance against Pakistan is a full-circle moment born from a career-altering injury
stories.what_happened: With Jacob Bethell now injured and unavailable, Jordan Cox has been promoted to bat at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan at Headingley — the very role once denied to him by injury, now his because of someone else's. Cox has spoken this week about drawing on advice from Virat Kohli, his former captain at Royal Challengers Bengaluru, who told him to focus on enjoying the occasion rather than being weighed down by its importance. Cox described the moment as bringing a sense of **"clarity"** to his game, even as it puts him in an unfamiliar top-order role for England, two years after the injury that first cost him this exact opportunity.
key_points: **Jordan Cox** is batting at number three for England's first Test against Pakistan, filling in for the injured **Jacob Bethell**.
It's a **full-circle moment**: Bethell's own Test debut two years ago only happened because Cox broke his thumb in the nets days before his scheduled debut.
Cox credits advice from **Virat Kohli**, his former Royal Challengers Bengaluru captain, for helping him handle the pressure of Test selection.
Kohli reportedly told Cox to **enjoy the occasion** rather than let its significance overwhelm him.
Cox finally made his delayed Test debut at **The Oval in June**, batting at number seven as cover for a suspended Ben Stokes.

depth.background: Jordan Cox was on the verge of a Test debut against New Zealand two years ago, only to fracture his thumb in the nets just days before the match — forcing him to call his own father and tell him not to fly out to watch. **Jacob Bethell** stepped into the vacated spot instead, and went on to build his own England Test career from that opportunity. Cox finally got his own Test debut this June, at The Oval, playing at number seven as cover while Ben Stokes served a suspension. He also spent time playing IPL cricket for **Royal Challengers Bengaluru**, where he crossed paths with Virat Kohli, one of the format's most storied players, who has become an unlikely mentor figure to him.

stories.title: US agencies say hackers are using AI-written code to break into the computers that run water plants
stories.what_happened: On **19 August 2026**, five US federal agencies — the National Security Agency, the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), the FBI, the Department of Energy and the Environmental Protection Agency — put out a **joint advisory** saying attackers are actively breaking into internet-facing Siemens S7 programmable logic controllers across the water, energy, chemical and manufacturing sectors. The agencies made a point of saying the intruders used **AI-generated exploitation scripts** — code written with the help of an AI model rather than by a human expert — which lowers the skill needed to attack this kind of equipment. In several cases the attackers **changed device passwords** so plant operators were locked out of their own controllers, and **altered IP addresses** so the machines dropped off the plant's network entirely. Officials have logged intrusions at water and wastewater facilities in **Minnesota, Michigan, Arkansas, Georgia and New Jersey**, and describe the recent activity as a significant escalation in both volume and boldness. The advisory tells operators to get these controllers off the open internet, change default credentials, and segment industrial networks from ordinary IT networks.
key_points: Five US agencies — NSA, CISA, FBI, Energy and EPA — issued a **joint alert**
Attackers used **AI-generated scripts** to exploit Siemens S7 controllers
Intrusions confirmed at water sites in **Minnesota, Michigan, Arkansas, Georgia and New Jersey**
Hackers **changed passwords and IP addresses**, locking operators out of their own equipment
Officials call it a **'significant escalation'** against internet-exposed industrial devices

depth.background: Water treatment plants, power stations and factories are not run by ordinary office computers. They are run by **programmable logic controllers (PLCs)** — small, rugged industrial computers that open valves, dose chemicals and start pumps on a fixed schedule. Siemens' **S7 series** is one of the most widely used PLC families in the world, and many of these devices were designed decades ago for closed, isolated networks — then quietly connected to the internet so engineers could check on them remotely. Small US water utilities, which often have **no dedicated cybersecurity staff**, are the softest targets in that picture, and federal agencies have been warning about exposed controllers at them for over two years.

stories.title: Asian chip stocks crash as 30-year US Treasury yields hit a 19-year high, with Samsung and SK Hynix both losing over 7%
stories.what_happened: Asian markets sold off sharply as trading opened on Wednesday, with **Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix** — the two biggest suppliers of memory chips to AI data centers — both losing more than **7%** of their value in a single session. The **KOSPI**, South Korea's benchmark index, fell so fast that the exchange had to **briefly halt trading** after a 5% slide. The proximate trigger was the **US 30-year Treasury yield surging to 5.33%**, its highest point since 2007, driven by a mix of escalating Middle East tensions (including the Strait of Hormuz standoff) and persistent worries about US government debt and inflation. Investors also cited growing skepticism about whether the **trillions of dollars** Big Tech is pouring into AI data centers and chips will generate returns fast enough to justify current stock prices. The damage wasn't confined to Korea — **MSCI's broader Asia-Pacific index** fell around 2% as the selloff spread across the region.
key_points: The **30-year US Treasury yield** jumped to **5.33%**, its highest level since **2007** — 19 years ago.
**Samsung Electronics** fell as much as **7.17%** and **SK Hynix** tumbled **8.42%**, dragging South Korea's market down.
South Korea's stock exchange **briefly halted trading** after the KOSPI index slid **5%** in a single session.
**MSCI's Asia-Pacific equities benchmark** slid about **2%** as the rout spread beyond Korean chipmakers.
The selloff blends **rising bond yields**, **Middle East tensions**, and doubts about whether massive **AI infrastructure spending** will ever pay off.

depth.background: A **Treasury yield** is the interest rate the US government pays to borrow money for a set period — 30 years, in this case. When that yield rises, it means investors are demanding more compensation to lend long-term, often because they expect higher inflation, more government borrowing, or more risk ahead. Higher yields matter enormously for **AI and chip stocks** specifically because their sky-high valuations are built on profits investors expect years from now — and the more it costs to borrow today, the less those distant future profits are worth in today's dollars. Samsung and SK Hynix are the world's two biggest makers of the memory chips that power AI data centers, so they sit at the center of the same AI-spending boom that has driven markets for the past two years.

stories.title: Meta's child-safety trial opens with a whistleblower now cleared to testify against the company
stories.what_happened: Opening statements began August 18 in the consolidated child-safety trial against Meta. California deputy attorney general Megan O'Neill argued Meta's core business model depends on exploiting the attention and data of young users, and that internally the company knew and hid the risks. Meta's lawyers are expected to counter that the company has built extensive parental-control and safety features and that youth mental health has many causes beyond social media. In a significant pretrial ruling, the judge denied Meta's motion to exclude **Arturo Bejar**, a former senior engineer who became a prominent whistleblower after telling the Senate in 2023 that Meta knew its platforms harmed teenagers and chose not to act. His testimony is now expected to feature prominently over the trial's six-plus weeks, alongside planned testimony from **Zuckerberg** himself and top Instagram executives.
key_points: The trial, in **US District Court in Northern California**, opened August 18 with attorneys general from **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** leading the case on behalf of **29 states** total.
California deputy AG **Megan O'Neill** told the court Meta's business "relies on exploiting young people's data and attention" and that it **lied about known risks** to teen mental health.

The judge refused Meta's request to bar former senior engineer and whistleblower **Arturo Bejar** from testifying — he told the US Senate in 2023 that Meta knew about harms to teens and failed to act.
The trial is expected to run **at least six weeks**, with testimony expected from **Mark Zuckerberg**, Instagram head **Adam Mosseri**, and Meta's global safety chief **Antigone Davis**.
Meta **denies the allegations** and is expected to argue it has invested heavily in safety tools and that broader youth mental-health trends aren't its doing.

depth.background: This case is the product of years of state-level investigations into how Instagram and Facebook are designed, following 2021 leaks (the "Facebook Files") showing Meta's own internal research found Instagram worsened body-image issues for a meaningful share of teen girls. Roughly **29 US states** sued Meta separately, and this trial — with four states as the lead plaintiffs — is the first to actually reach a courtroom. The stakes are unusually high: penalties and damages sought could theoretically total **$1.4 trillion**, though such maximalist figures rarely survive intact even when plaintiffs win.

thread.previously: We reported the trial opened this week, with a coalition of US state attorneys general accusing Meta of deliberately engineering Instagram to be addictive to teenagers, in a case that could cost the company up to $1.4 trillion.
thread.changed: Opening statements were delivered on August 18: a California deputy attorney general laid out the states' core allegation that Meta's business model depends on exploiting kids' data and attention, and the judge rejected Meta's attempt to block whistleblower Arturo Bejar from testifying — a ruling that lets the trial's most damaging insider witness take the stand.

stories.title: Rescuers recover the last two bodies from Uttarakhand's Chamoli tunnel collapse, toll now at 10
stories.what_happened: On August 13, a landslide-triggered surge of water and debris flooded the under-construction tunnel at Hat-Siyasain, Mayapur-Pipalkoti, trapping 22 workers inside. Twelve were rescued with injuries in the days that followed as India's State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) and National Disaster Response Force (NDRF) mounted an intensive search-and-rescue operation. Bodies were recovered in stages over the following days, and on August 18 the last two — identified as Lukas Topno and Chetan Poyam — were found, bringing the confirmed death toll to 10 and formally concluding the search operation.
key_points: The bodies of **Lukas Topno** (31, from Jharkhand) and **Chetan Poyam** (from Chhattisgarh) were the last of **22 trapped workers** to be found
A landslide flooded the tunnel with debris and water on **August 13**, at a hydro-project site near the Birhi river
**12 workers were rescued** with injuries; the confirmed death toll now stands at **10**
The tunnel belongs to the **Vishnugad-Pipalkoti hydroelectric project**, run by state-owned THDC India
**SDRF and NDRF** teams, working what officials called a war-footing operation, have formally concluded the search

depth.background: Uttarakhand's stretch of the Himalayas is geologically young and prone to sudden landslides, especially during the monsoon, which makes large infrastructure projects there — like hydroelectric dams and their access tunnels — inherently risky to build. The workforce on such projects is often made up of migrant laborers from poorer states like Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh, who take on dangerous jobs far from home. The August 13 accident happened inside a **three-kilometre tunnel** under construction for the Vishnugad-Pipalkoti hydro project when a landslide near the Birhi river sent a sudden surge of debris and water inside, trapping the 22 workers who were on shift.

stories.title: AI chip startup Etched doubles its valuation to $21 billion in under a month
stories.what_happened: Etched announced it raised **$700 million** in a funding round led by **Jane Street**, valuing the company at **$21 billion** — nearly double its **$10.3 billion** valuation from just one month earlier. Jane Street, a major trading firm, is also Etched's first customer and received its first rack of Etched's AI hardware last month, which is now running live workloads. Etched says the AI chips it builds are designed specifically for **inference** — running trained AI models efficiently — rather than for training new ones, aiming to make it cheaper for companies to actually deploy AI products at scale. The company says it has signed more than **$1 billion** in contracts with AI companies and cloud providers.
key_points: Etched raised **$700 million** at a **$21 billion** valuation, led by trading firm Jane Street.
Its valuation has **more than doubled in about a month** — it was $10.3 billion in July and just $5 billion last December.
The company builds chips specialized for AI **'inference'** — running already-trained models — not for training them.
Etched says it has already signed **over $1 billion** in customer contracts across AI companies and cloud providers.
Jane Street, its first customer, put its first rack of Etched hardware into production last month.

depth.background: Most of the AI chip boom so far has been about **training** — the expensive, one-time process of teaching a model, dominated by Nvidia. Etched, a San Jose startup, is betting the next bottleneck is **inference**: the ongoing, everyday cost of actually running a trained model to answer a query, generate an image, or power an AI agent — a cost companies pay every single time someone uses the product. Etched's valuation has climbed at an unusual pace: **$5 billion in December**, **$10.3 billion in a Series C this past July**, and now **$21 billion**, reflecting investor belief that specialized chips built only for inference can run AI dramatically cheaper and faster than general-purpose chips.

stories.title: Former Fauci adviser David Morens pleads guilty to hiding Covid-era records
stories.what_happened: Morens entered a guilty plea to a **single conspiracy charge** at a federal court hearing in **Greenbelt, Maryland**. Prosecutors alleged he deliberately routed sensitive messages through his **personal email account** to keep them out of reach of public-records requests the agency was receiving about Covid-19 research grants. The alleged conduct began in **April 2020**, early in the pandemic. He now faces a maximum of **five years in prison** and will be **sentenced on Nov 12**. Prosecutors were careful to note they have **not accused Anthony Fauci** of any wrongdoing in connection with the case.
key_points: David Morens, **78**, a top ex-adviser to Anthony Fauci, pleaded guilty to a **conspiracy** charge.
Prosecutors say he used a **private email** to dodge public-records law.
The records concerned **Covid-19 research grants** during the pandemic.
He faces up to **five years** in prison; sentencing is **Nov 12**.
Fauci himself has **not been accused** of any wrongdoing here.

depth.background: In the US, a law called **FOIA (the Freedom of Information Act)** lets the public request government documents; officials aren't allowed to hide records to avoid it. Morens was a senior official at the **National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)**, the agency Fauci led during the pandemic. He was **indicted in April** over what prosecutors described as a scheme, starting in **April 2020**, to thwart records requests tied to Covid research funding. The case has become politically charged because it touches the still-contested question of how Covid-related grant money was handled.

stories.title: NASA images reveal a 60-foot crater where a discarded SpaceX rocket stage slammed into the Moon
stories.what_happened: The rocket stage struck the Moon on **August 5, 2026**, slamming into the surface at an estimated **5,400 miles per hour**. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO), a satellite that has been circling and mapping the Moon since 2009, flew over the impact site on **August 11 and 12** and photographed the aftermath — engineers had to tilt the spacecraft's cameras while it moved at **1 mile per second**, 60 miles above the surface, just to get a clean shot. NASA released the before-and-after images on **Tuesday, August 18**, showing a fresh crater roughly **60 feet wide** gouged into the lunar dust. It is the clearest confirmed picture yet of a piece of Earth-launched hardware hitting the Moon.
key_points: A defunct **Falcon 9 upper stage** hit the Moon on **August 5** at roughly **5,400 mph**.
NASA's **Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter** photographed the site on **August 11-12**, six days after the crash.
The impact carved a fresh crater about **60 feet (18 meters) wide** into the lunar surface.
Engineers had to **tilt the orbiter** mid-flight, 60 miles up, so its camera could catch the crater.
The stage began its journey in **January 2025**, launching two commercial Moon landers before being discarded.

depth.background: In January 2025, a **SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket** launched two commercial lunar landers into space. Once its job was done, the rocket's spent upper stage — the second, smaller segment that fires after the main booster falls away — was released into orbit, as is routine after most launches. Nobody aimed it at the Moon on purpose; instead, the **slow drift of orbital mechanics** — the gravitational tug-of-war between Earth, the Moon, and the Sun — gradually bent its path until it was on a certain collision course, a phenomenon astronomers had been tracking and predicting for months.

stories.title: Racing Bulls tells its two title-hopeful rookies they can race flat-out — with one rule: don't touch
stories.what_happened: Team principal Alan Permane confirmed that Racing Bulls will **not impose team orders** to protect one driver over the other, even though Lawson and Lindblad are directly competing with each other for results, for a place ahead of Tsolov in the pecking order, and ultimately for a possible Red Bull promotion. The only boundary Permane set is that the two must **not make contact** with each other while racing. Permane said the team expects to arrive at this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort '**even stronger**' than before the summer break.
key_points: Racing Bulls boss **Alan Permane** set just one rule for teammates **Liam Lawson** and **Arvid Lindblad**: don't touch each other.
The team is chasing its **best-ever Constructors' Championship finish** and won't order either driver to back off.
Both drivers are also racing for a possible future **Red Bull seat**, adding personal stakes to every on-track battle.
F2 champion **Nikola Tsolov** is a further threat to both drivers' longer-term F1 futures.
Permane says the team expects to come back **'even stronger' at Zandvoort** this weekend.

depth.background: Racing Bulls is Red Bull's sister/junior team, and this season it is fighting for its **best-ever finish** in the Constructors' Championship — the team title based on combined points from both drivers. Teammates **Liam Lawson** and 18-year-old rookie **Arvid Lindblad** are not just racing for the team; they are also both competing for the same prize of a future promotion to the senior **Red Bull** team if a seat opens up, with rising Formula 2 champion **Nikola Tsolov** also in the wings as a longer-term threat to both their prospects.

stories.title: India clears field trials of 1 billion ₹10 and ₹20 polymer banknotes
stories.what_happened: India's government told **Parliament** it has cleared the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** to conduct **field trials of one billion polymer banknotes each in the ₹10 and ₹20 denominations**. Officials stressed the goal is to **extend the lifespan** of small notes that wear out fastest, **reduce long-term printing costs**, and cut environmental waste. Crucially, they clarified there is **no plan to replace paper currency** — the polymer notes would circulate **alongside** existing paper notes, not instead of them. The move follows international studies showing polymer notes are significantly more durable than paper.
key_points: The government approved the **RBI's plan** to field-test **plastic (polymer) notes**.
The trial covers **one billion notes each** of **₹10 and ₹20**.
Aim: notes that **last far longer** than paper, cutting reprinting costs.
Paper currency **will continue** alongside — no plan to replace it.
Small notes wear out fastest, so they're the natural test case.

depth.background: Low-value notes like **₹10 and ₹20** change hands constantly, so they get grubby and torn quickly and have to be reprinted often — which is expensive and wasteful. **Polymer notes** are made of a thin, durable plastic film instead of cotton-paper; countries like Australia and the UK already use them because they **last two to three times longer** and are harder to counterfeit. India has floated the idea before (going back years) but never rolled it out at scale. This decision moves it from proposal to an actual **field trial** — a real-world test in limited circulation.

stories.title: Meta goes on trial today in a case that could cost it up to $1.4 trillion over child safety
stories.what_happened: Opening statements began Tuesday, **August 18**, in a California federal courtroom, kicking off what is expected to be a **six-to-eight-week trial**. Attorneys general from **California, Colorado, Kentucky, and New Jersey** are leading the case on behalf of the 29 states, arguing Meta built features like infinite scroll and push notifications specifically to maximize the time children spend on its apps. The states are asking for financial penalties that could theoretically reach **$1.4 trillion**, along with court-ordered changes to how Meta designs and operates Facebook and Instagram. Meta CEO **Mark Zuckerberg**, along with other current and former executives, is expected to take the stand during the trial.
key_points: **29 US states** sued Meta in 2023, accusing it of designing Instagram and Facebook features that deliberately hook children.
Opening arguments began **August 18** in an Oakland federal court before Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers.
States are seeking damages that could total as much as **$1.4 trillion**, plus forced changes to how Meta runs its apps.
The trial is expected to run **six to eight weeks**, with **Mark Zuckerberg** among the executives set to testify.
A separate group of **25 more states** has its own child-safety case against Meta still waiting for trial.

depth.background: Twenty-nine US states filed suit against Meta in **2023**, arguing the company knowingly built addictive features into Instagram and Facebook that fueled a youth mental-health crisis, and that it collected data on children under 13 without parental consent in violation of federal privacy law. Meta has faced years of similar accusations from parents, researchers, and its own former employees, some of whom have testified that internal research showed the company knew its products harmed teenagers' wellbeing. This is the **first of the 29-state cases to reach trial**; a related group of 25 additional states is pursuing its own case separately. A federal jury already ordered Meta to pay **$375 million** in a related child-safety verdict earlier this year.

stories.title: FIA sets August 25 court date for McLaren and Red Bull's appeal over Gasly's overturned Monaco penalties
stories.what_happened: McLaren and Red Bull, whose drivers were affected by Gasly's promotion, jointly lodged a formal appeal with the FIA against both of the stewards' decisions from that Monaco weekend (**Case ICA-2026-06-07-08-09**, over Document 99 issued June 12). The FIA has now confirmed the **International Court of Appeal** will hear the case on **August 25 at 09:00 local time in Paris**, at FIA headquarters. Both sides asked for the hearing to be held behind closed doors, so the arguments won't be public, but the FIA says it will publish a written decision as soon as possible afterward.
key_points: The **FIA's International Court of Appeal** will hear the case in **Paris on August 25** at 09:00 local time.
**McLaren and Red Bull** are jointly appealing a decision that wiped out **Pierre Gasly's** pit-lane speeding penalties from the **Monaco Grand Prix**.
Gasly was originally penalized for two pit-lane speeds of **60.1 km/h and 60.4 km/h**, breaching the pit-lane speed limit rule.
**Alpine** successfully used its 'Right of Review' to get those penalties overturned, promoting Gasly to **3rd place**.
The hearing will be held **behind closed doors** at both teams' request; a ruling follows afterward.

depth.background: Monaco's pit lane has one of F1's strictest speed limits because its exit merges directly with a blind, narrow racing line, making speeding there a real safety risk rather than just a technicality. During the June Monaco GP, stewards penalized Alpine's Pierre Gasly for exceeding that limit twice. Alpine later invoked its **'Right of Review'** — a formal process teams can use to ask stewards to revisit a decision if new evidence emerges — and succeeded in getting the penalties thrown out, which bumped Gasly up to third place at the expense of drivers who had finished ahead of him under the original penalties.

stories.title: Antonelli returns from the break with a 50-point title cushion, but Hamilton's Ferrari has closed the gap
stories.what_happened: F1 returns from its summer break with Antonelli still on top of the standings on **219 points**, a **50-point cushion** over Hamilton in second and Russell close behind in third. But the underlying form tells a different story: Antonelli's results over his last five races rank only fourth in the field, while **Ferrari has won two of the last five grands prix** and **McLaren finally converted its car's potential into a win in Hungary** — its first victory of the season. That combination has shifted the narrative from "is this a runaway title" to a genuine, if still Antonelli-favored, fight over the season's remaining **12 races**, starting with this weekend's Zandvoort finale for the circuit.
key_points: **Kimi Antonelli** leads the championship with **219 points** after 11 races — a **50-point lead** over second-placed Lewis Hamilton.
**George Russell** sits third, a further six points behind Hamilton, keeping Mercedes in the mix at the top.
Antonelli has **6 wins, 6 poles and 9 podiums** so far, but his form over the last five races ranks only **fourth-best** in the field.
**Ferrari has won two of the last five races** and **McLaren won for the first time in 2026 in Hungary**, both signs the title fight is tightening.
Bookmakers still favor Antonelli heavily (around 1/4), with Hamilton next (about 6/1) as F1 resumes at Zandvoort with **12 races remaining**.

depth.background: Kimi Antonelli, racing for Mercedes, opened the 2026 season as a breakout title contender, winning five of the early races and prompting fears the championship could turn into a runaway. Since then, Mercedes has hit reliability issues, and 43-year-old **Lewis Hamilton** — now in his second full season at Ferrari after leaving Mercedes — has found late-career form, closing what once looked like a comfortable gap. The sport's mandatory mid-season **summer break** gives every team a moment to reset, and this weekend's return at Zandvoort kicks off the second half of the season with the title picture more competitive than it looked at the year's midpoint.

stories.title: Milky Mist Dairy shares jump 18% on debut, hit the upper circuit after a blockbuster IPO
stories.what_happened: Milky Mist Dairy Food debuted on India's stock exchanges on **August 18**, with shares opening at **Rs 165 apiece**, an 18% premium over its Rs 140 issue price. The stock extended gains after listing, hitting the **10% upper circuit at Rs 181.45** on the BSE. The Rs 1,553-crore public offer had drawn strong demand, closing **56.12 times subscribed** overall — bids came in for over 4.59 billion shares against roughly 818 million on offer. Qualified institutional buyers subscribed their portion 155.83 times, non-institutional investors 34.91 times, and retail investors 8.41 times. At its debut price, the company commands a market capitalization of about **Rs 12,702 crore**.
key_points: Milky Mist Dairy Food shares **listed at Rs 165**, an **18% premium** over the Rs 140 issue price, on both NSE and BSE.
The stock then hit its **10% upper circuit at Rs 181.45**, meaning trading was capped after gaining the maximum allowed for the day.
The **Rs 1,553-crore IPO** was subscribed **56 times over**, with bids for 4.59 billion shares against 818 million on offer.
Institutional investors led demand, subscribing their portion **155.8 times**, versus 34.9 times for non-institutional and 8.4 times for retail.
At the listing price, Milky Mist is valued at roughly **Rs 12,702 crore** (about $1.5 billion).

depth.background: Milky Mist is an Indian **packaged dairy and food company**, competing in a segment that includes players like Amul and Britannia as India's branded-food market grows with rising incomes and urbanization. An **IPO (initial public offering)** is when a private company sells shares to the public for the first time to raise money and list on a stock exchange; how eagerly investors bid for those shares — the **'subscription' level** — is a widely watched signal of market appetite. Strong dairy and consumer-staples IPOs have been relatively rare in a year when India's broader stock market has been volatile on global cues.

stories.title: Sensex and Nifty slide as the Iran ceasefire lapses and oil jumps — why costlier crude hits India harder than most
stories.what_happened: Indian equity markets fell for a second straight session as the US-Iran ceasefire's expiry revived fears of prolonged Middle East conflict disrupting oil supply. The **Sensex slid 278 points to 77,451**, while the **Nifty 50 dropped 0.24% to 24,230**, extending losses from the previous close. **Brent crude pushed above $91 a barrel** and US crude (WTI) rose toward **$85**, both reflecting worry that fighting could threaten tanker traffic near the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping route. IT stocks were hit hardest — the sector is especially exposed to global risk sentiment and a weaker rupee cuts both ways for exporters — with the **Nifty IT index down 1.24%** and heavyweights Infosys, TCS, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra all trading lower. The rupee weakened further and India's volatility index (India VIX) ticked up, both signs of rising investor nervousness.
key_points: The **Sensex fell 278 points** and the **Nifty 50 dropped below 24,250** in Tuesday trading as Middle East tensions spooked investors.
**Brent crude climbed above $91 a barrel** after the US-Iran ceasefire expired with no extension in sight, reviving fears that fighting could disrupt oil supply.
**IT stocks led the losses** — the Nifty IT index fell **1.24%**, with Infosys, TCS, HCLTech and Tech Mahindra all down — alongside a weaker rupee and rising global bond yields.
India imports the large majority of the crude oil it uses, so pricier oil directly threatens its import bill, inflation and corporate margins.

depth.background: India is one of the world's largest oil importers and buys the vast majority of the crude it consumes from abroad, so global oil-price swings hit its economy faster and harder than economies that produce more of their own energy. Indian stock indices — the **Sensex** (30 major companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange) and the **Nifty 50** (50 major companies on the National Stock Exchange) — are the two benchmarks used to gauge how Indian equity markets are doing overall. Oil-price spikes tend to hit India through multiple channels at once: a bigger import bill, a weaker rupee (since more dollars are needed to pay for oil), and higher inflation that can force the central bank to keep interest rates elevated.

stories.title: Australia axes Jake Weatherald after the 'Darwin disaster', recalls Matt Renshaw — and gives Marnus Labuschagne one more Test to save his spot
stories.what_happened: Following the nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin — Australia's first-ever Test defeat to Bangladesh — national selectors dropped opening batter Jake Weatherald, who scored 23 and 0 in the match, and recalled Matt Renshaw for the second Test in Mackay. Marnus Labuschagne, who managed only 1 and 31 at No.3, keeps his place in the squad, but head coach Andrew McDonald publicly acknowledged the right-hander has work to do to hold his spot going forward. The fallout from the Darwin loss was compounded by photos of players golfing during the post-match period, which drew criticism from fans and commentators questioning the squad's focus.
key_points: **Jake Weatherald** is dropped after scoring **23 and 0** in the shock Darwin loss to Bangladesh, replaced by **Matt Renshaw** for the second Test.
It's Australia's **first-ever Test defeat to Bangladesh**, a genuine shock result that triggered the selection shake-up.
**Marnus Labuschagne** survives for now despite managing just **1 and 31**, but coach Andrew McDonald says he still has work to do to secure his No.3 spot.
The axing follows public backlash after photos surfaced of players golfing in the aftermath of the loss.

depth.background: Australia's men's Test team is one of the most successful sides in cricket history, which is exactly why losing a Test to Bangladesh — a side Australia had never lost to before in the format — landed as such a shock. No.3 is traditionally the most important specialist batting position after the openers, requiring a player who can handle the new ball early while anchoring the innings; Marnus Labuschagne has held that role for Australia for several years but has been out of form for an extended stretch, averaging just over 25 across his last 22 Tests without a century in that span.

thread.previously: After a shock nine-wicket loss to Bangladesh in Darwin — a first-ever Test defeat to Bangladesh for Australia — selectors were reportedly weighing batting changes, with anger further stoked by photos of players golfing during the fallout.
thread.changed: Selectors have now actually dropped opener **Jake Weatherald**, who made just 23 and 0 in Darwin, and recalled **Matt Renshaw** for the second Test in Mackay. **Marnus Labuschagne** — who scored only 1 and 31 — keeps his No.3 spot for now, but coach Andrew McDonald has openly said he has work to do to hold onto it.

stories.title: OpenAI launches 'ChatGPT for Teens' with age checks and parental controls, its first major response to child-safety lawsuits
stories.what_happened: OpenAI officially launched **"ChatGPT for Teens"** on August 18, a separate, age-gated version of its chatbot built specifically for users aged **13 to 17**. The teen version blocks content related to self-harm, suicide, eating disorders, and violent or sexual material, and the model is barred from using romantic language or implying it has feelings toward a teen user. OpenAI paired the launch with a new **age-prediction/verification system** to detect underage users on the standard product, plus parental controls including "Quiet Hours" that limit access at set times, safety notifications to parents, and the ability to link a parent and teen account together. The company also added a **"Study Mode"** designed to walk teens through problems step by step rather than simply handing over answers. The launch was reported the same day by Axios, AP (syndicated via ABC News), TechCrunch, the Washington Post, and Fortune, and comes as OpenAI faces an active wrongful-death lawsuit and rising state-level regulatory pressure over harm to minors — in the same week Meta enters a 29-state trial over youth mental-health harms tied to its own platforms.
key_points: OpenAI rolled out a separate, age-gated version of ChatGPT for users **13–17**, with new content restrictions and an age-prediction system
The teen version **blocks self-harm, suicide, eating-disorder, and sexual/romantic content**, and bars the bot from using romantic language
New **parental controls** let guardians set "Quiet Hours," get safety notifications, and link accounts to their teen's
It arrives amid a **wrongful-death lawsuit** and state attorney-general scrutiny over AI chatbot harm to minors
The launch lands the same week Meta heads into a related **29-state trial** over youth mental-health harms from its platforms

depth.background: ChatGPT has been used by tens of millions of teenagers since its 2022 launch, even though OpenAI's terms technically required users to be 13 or older with parental consent for under-18s, with no real age-verification system in place. Over the past two years, several families have filed lawsuits against AI chatbot makers — including one wrongful-death suit against OpenAI — alleging that chatbots engaged in harmful, sometimes sexualized or self-harm-normalizing conversations with minors. Regulators, including several US state attorneys general, have been publicly pressing AI companies to build in stronger youth-safety protections, echoing the scrutiny social media platforms faced a decade earlier.

stories.title: Joe Root scraps England's midnight curfew for the Pakistan Tests, and Nasser Hussain calls it 'a grown-up decision'
stories.what_happened: Root abolished the team's midnight curfew as his first act back as captain, telling players to behave like **'grown adults'** instead of policing them with a fixed rule. Former England captain **Nasser Hussain** endorsed the move on the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast, calling it **'just a grown-up decision'** and arguing that if players don't act responsibly, the right response is to **fine them first, and drop them if it continues** — rather than impose blanket restrictions on the whole squad. Hussain added that needing a curfew in the first place 'shows how bad a place they were in.' The change comes as Root leads England into the opening Test of a three-match series against Pakistan at Headingley, his first Test in charge since 2022.
key_points: Root scrapped the **midnight curfew** in his **first act since returning as England Test captain**.
The curfew was brought in after **Ben Stokes and Gus Atkinson broke it**, missing a Test after a nightclub incident.
Former captain **Nasser Hussain** backed the call, saying **'a professional sporting outfit shouldn't need a curfew.'**
Root wants players treated as **'grown adults'**, with fines and then being dropped as the real deterrent instead of blanket rules.

depth.background: England's Test team introduced player-behaviour guidelines, including a midnight curfew, after a string of off-field alcohol-related incidents during the **'Bazball' era**. The rule became a flashpoint when then-captain **Ben Stokes and bowler Gus Atkinson** were left out of a Test against New Zealand after being caught breaking it following a nightclub visit. **Joe Root** has now returned to the England Test captaincy for a second stint — having previously stepped down in 2022 — and this Pakistan series, starting today at Headingley, is his first assignment back in charge.

stories.title: IMD issues red alert for Odisha and Jharkhand as a Bengal depression brings heavy rain to 25 states
stories.what_happened: A **depression forming over the Bay of Bengal** has triggered the IMD's most serious warning level — a **red alert** — for parts of Odisha and Jharkhand, where isolated pockets could see more than **20 cm of rain in a single day**, enough to cause flash flooding. Hilly northern states — Jammu & Kashmir, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand — are under an **orange alert**, with forecasters warning heavy rain could trigger landslides, flash floods, and disruption to mountain roads. More broadly, the IMD has issued rain and thunderstorm warnings covering **25 states and Union Territories**, with wind gusts up to **65 kmph** in some areas. Delhi-NCR is expecting cloudy skies with light showers, while Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal, and eastern Madhya Pradesh are all bracing for a heavier downpour.
key_points: The **India Meteorological Department (IMD)** issued a **red alert** for parts of Odisha and Jharkhand.
Isolated areas could see **over 20 cm of rainfall within 24 hours**.
An **orange alert** covers J&K, Himachal Pradesh, and Uttarakhand, warning of landslides and flash floods.
Heavy rain and thunderstorm warnings apply to **25 states and Union Territories**, with winds up to 65 kmph.
Delhi-NCR, UP, Bihar, West Bengal, and eastern Madhya Pradesh are all under some level of alert.

depth.background: India's monsoon (roughly June to September) brings the bulk of the country's annual rainfall, and it periodically intensifies into short, sharp 'depressions' — low-pressure weather systems over the Bay of Bengal that pull in moisture and dump it on land as they move inland. The IMD uses a four-colour alert system (green, yellow, orange, red) to flag how severe and how urgent a weather threat is, with red meaning 'take action' — the highest level, reserved for conditions expected to cause significant disruption or danger.

stories.title: Adani Enterprises becomes India's best Nifty 50 stock of 2026, up 34%, after a US court drops fraud charges
stories.what_happened: Adani Enterprises has climbed **34% so far in 2026**, reclaiming the position of the **best-performing stock on the Nifty 50** index. The rally accelerated after a **US federal judge permanently dismissed** the securities fraud charges that had been filed against Adani Group executives, closing out a legal overhang that dated back to 2024. Separately, global index provider **MSCI** raised the free-float factor — the share of a company's stock considered available for public trading — for several Adani group companies in its latest review, a technical change that forces passive index funds tracking MSCI benchmarks to buy more Adani stock. **Morgan Stanley** had already initiated coverage on the stock in June with an 'overweight' (buy) rating.
key_points: Adani Enterprises has risen **34% in 2026**, making it the **top-performing Nifty 50 stock** this year.
A **US federal judge permanently dismissed** the securities fraud case against Adani executives.
**MSCI** raised the free-float weighting of several Adani companies, forcing global index funds to buy more of the stock.
**Morgan Stanley** initiated coverage in June with an 'overweight' rating, backing further gains.
The rally marks a comeback from the **2023 Hindenburg report** that had wiped out over $150 billion in Adani Group value.

depth.background: Adani Enterprises, the flagship company of billionaire **Gautam Adani's** conglomerate, was at the center of India's biggest corporate governance storm in years after US short-seller **Hindenburg Research** accused the group of stock manipulation and accounting fraud in **2023**, erasing over $150 billion in market value at its worst point. The group was later hit with a **2024 US indictment** alleging a bribery scheme tied to solar energy contracts, which kept foreign investors wary and the stock under a cloud for nearly two years. Adani has consistently denied all wrongdoing.

stories.title: A ship is struck by an 'unknown projectile' in the Strait of Hormuz, wounding a crew member, hours after Iran vows to go 'fully offensive'
stories.what_happened: The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre (UKMTO) reported that a vessel was struck by an **unknown projectile** while transiting outbound through the Strait of Hormuz at **01:35 UTC on August 18**, causing **engine room damage and a crew casualty** — it remains unclear whether the crew member was killed or wounded. The rest of the crew was assisted by the **Omani Coast Guard**. No group has claimed responsibility, and authorities are still investigating who or what fired the projectile. Hours later, President Trump posted on Truth Social that the strait is **'open and operating'** and that 'all water mines have been removed or detonated,' while also saying there are **no talks scheduled** with Tehran. US Central Command declined to confirm his demining claim and referred questions to the White House. Iran's top negotiator countered that the strait will **not reopen** until the US lifts its naval blockade and releases frozen Iranian assets — directly contradicting Trump's account.
key_points: A vessel was hit by an **unknown projectile** exiting the Strait of Hormuz at **01:35 UTC**, damaging its engine room.
**One crew member was hurt**; survivors were assisted by the **Omani Coast Guard**, per the UK's UKMTO monitor.
**No group has claimed responsibility** — the attack came hours after Iran declared a 'fully offensive' posture.
Trump posted the strait is **'open and operating'**, but **US Central Command would not confirm** his claim that mines were cleared.
Iran's top negotiator says the strait **stays shut** until the US lifts its naval blockade and unfreezes Iranian assets.

depth.background: The **Strait of Hormuz** is the narrow waterway between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** passes through by tanker — there is no practical detour. A 60-day US-Iran ceasefire (the Islamabad Memorandum) lapsed on **August 16** with no permanent deal on Iran's nuclear program, and Iranian officials told Reuters the same day that Tehran was formally shifting from a defensive posture to a **'fully offensive'** one in the strait. Weekly ship transits had already fallen from 118 to 95 as owners grew wary of the chokepoint even before this strike.

thread.previously: We reported Iran had formally declared a shift from a defensive to a 'fully offensive' posture in the strait after its ceasefire with the US lapsed, warning it was ready for a 'timely and precise' military attack to break the US naval blockade, while ship transits had already begun falling.
thread.changed: That declared posture has now produced an actual attack: a vessel was hit by an unclaimed projectile and a crew member hurt, and the US and Iran are now giving directly contradictory public accounts of whether the strait is safe to use at all.

stories.title: Alex Albon extends his Williams contract through the 2027 F1 season
stories.what_happened: Williams announced on **Tuesday, August 18** that **Alex Albon** has extended his contract to cover the **2027 F1 season**, making it his sixth consecutive year with the team and eighth season in Formula 1 overall. Albon, 30, already had a multi-year deal that was believed to extend into 2027, but this announcement specifically resolves **exit clauses** in that contract, formally committing both sides rather than leaving 2027 as an option either party could walk away from. Albon set a new team record this season, making his **100th start for Williams** at the Hungarian Grand Prix in Budapest — the most grand prix starts by any driver in the team's history. The announcement came in the same week Williams also confirmed **Carlos Sainz** for 2027, meaning the team has now locked in both of its race seats well ahead of the usual driver-market rush later in the year.
key_points: **Alex Albon** signed a contract extension with **Williams** on Tuesday, keeping him at the team through **2027**.
It will be his **sixth season with Williams** and **eighth in Formula 1** overall.
Albon made his **100th start for Williams** in Budapest this season, the most of any driver in the team's history.
The move mainly confirms **exit clauses**, since his existing multi-year deal already covered 2027.
It comes in the same week Williams also locked in **Carlos Sainz** for 2027, settling both of its race seats early.

depth.background: **Williams** is one of Formula 1's oldest and most storied teams, currently in the middle of a long rebuild after years of struggling near the back of the grid. **Alex Albon** joined Williams in 2022 after being dropped by Red Bull, and has become central to the team's recovery, frequently out-performing the car's raw pace. Driver contracts in F1 often include **exit clauses** — conditions under which either the driver or team can leave a multi-year deal early — so confirmations like this one are as much about removing uncertainty as signing something brand new.

stories.title: Cadillac sacks team boss Graeme Lowdon, hands the reins to Marcin Budkowski
stories.what_happened: Cadillac announced that **Marcin Budkowski** will take over as team principal, replacing **Graeme Lowdon**, in what the team is calling a "planned leadership transition." CEO **Dan Towriss** made clear the decision was his alone, saying he had spent months searching for a new team boss to guide Cadillac's next phase of development — not something Lowdon signed off on as a mutual exit. The timing is notable: Cadillac remains the **only team on the 2026 grid without a single point** after 11 races, well behind schedule for a new entrant trying to establish itself. Budkowski, a 49-year-old Polish-French engineer, previously worked as **Alpine's executive director** until leaving that post in 2022, giving him senior team-management experience elsewhere on the grid. His first race in the new role will be the **Dutch Grand Prix** at Zandvoort (August 21-23), as F1 returns from its summer break.
key_points: Cadillac has replaced team principal **Graeme Lowdon** with **Marcin Budkowski**, effective immediately.
Cadillac CEO **Dan Towriss** says it was his call, not a mutual decision — he wanted a leadership change for the team's next phase.
Cadillac is the **only F1 team yet to score a point** after 11 rounds of its debut 2026 season.
Budkowski, 49, last worked in F1 as **Alpine's executive director**, a role he left in 2022.
His first race in charge is the **Dutch Grand Prix** (Aug 21-23), as F1 resumes from its summer break.

depth.background: **Cadillac** is Formula 1's newest team, debuting in the 2026 season as the sport's 11th entry after years of effort to join the grid. **Graeme Lowdon** was announced as its team boss ahead of that debut, tasked with building the operation from scratch. Cadillac is backed by **Dan Towriss**, CEO of TWG Motorsports, who has been closely involved in decisions about the team's leadership and direction as it tries to establish itself against long-established rivals.

stories.title: UK PM Andy Burnham says he wasn't fooled for long by a fake Trump chief of staff texting him
stories.what_happened: Andy Burnham, who leads the UK government, exchanged a small number of text messages with a person who was posing as Susie Wiles. Burnham said the content exchanged was trivial and of **no real significance**, but partway through the conversation he began to suspect the person wasn't who they claimed to be. Once suspicious, the **UK Embassy in Washington raised the matter with the White House** directly rather than letting the exchange continue. Speaking publicly on **Tuesday, August 18**, Burnham said he was **not embarrassed** by the episode and that he believed he'd handled it the right way by disengaging and reporting it. The White House and Trump himself downplayed the incident, with Trump insisting there's only one genuine Susie Wiles.
key_points: UK Prime Minister **Andy Burnham** exchanged a handful of messages with someone impersonating **Susie Wiles**, Trump's White House chief of staff.
Burnham says the messages traded were **"of no significance"** and he grew suspicious partway through the exchange.
The **UK Embassy in Washington** flagged the incident directly to the White House once Burnham realized something was off.
It's part of a **wider phishing campaign** targeting people connected to Wiles that the **FBI has been investigating since May 2025**.
Trump publicly shrugged it off, telling reporters **"there's only one Susie."**

depth.background: Susie Wiles is Donald Trump's White House chief of staff — effectively the person who controls what reaches the president's desk, making her one of the most powerful, and most impersonated, targets in Washington. Since **May 2025**, US law enforcement has been probing a campaign in which scammers spoofed Wiles' phone number and contact list to message senior officials, governors, and now apparently a foreign head of government. Wiles herself has said she believes her personal phone and contacts were **hacked** at some point, which is how the impersonators got a plausible-looking starting point. Burnham became UK prime minister earlier this year, making him a fresh, high-value target for anyone probing what a national leader might reveal to someone they believe is a top Trump aide.

stories.title: Ebola outbreak in Congo and Uganda becomes the fastest-growing on record, topping 5,000 cases
stories.what_happened: In just over three months since being declared a PHEIC, this Ebola outbreak has grown faster than any previous one on record. As of the WHO's August 18 update, confirmed cases stand at 5,021 with 2,378 deaths, concentrated in DRC's Ituri province (4,257 cases, 1,878 deaths) but now confirmed in North Kivu, South Kivu, and three other provinces. Uganda has also reported cases linked to the same outbreak. In response, five Central African countries — DRC, Uganda, the Central African Republic, the Republic of the Congo, and South Sudan — are coordinating tighter border surveillance and information-sharing to try to stop the virus crossing into new territory.
key_points: The WHO reports **5,021 confirmed cases** and **2,378 deaths** as of August 18 — a fatality rate near **47%**
The outbreak has spread from Ituri province to **five more provinces**, including North Kivu and South Kivu
WHO declared a **Public Health Emergency of International Concern (PHEIC)** on May 17; it's now the **fastest-growing Ebola outbreak on record**
**Five Central African nations** are tightening cross-border surveillance to stop further spread
The strain is **Bundibugyo virus**, striking remote, hard-to-reach areas of DRC and Uganda where conflict complicates the response

depth.background: Ebola causes severe fever and internal bleeding and has repeatedly emerged from this part of Central Africa, where past outbreaks — including the 2018-2020 DRC epidemic — showed how armed conflict and mistrust of health workers can let a virus spread for months before it's contained. A **PHEIC** is the World Health Organization's highest alarm level, reserved for outbreaks serious enough to need a coordinated global response; declaring one in May was meant to fast-track funding and expert deployment. Response efforts are also being complicated by recent cuts to US health-aid programs (CDC and USAID), which have historically funded much of the region's outbreak response.

stories.title: Ukraine fires nearly 800 drones at Moscow region in one of its largest attacks of the war
stories.what_happened: Overnight, Ukraine launched close to **800 drones** toward the Moscow region in what Russian officials called the second-largest such attack since January 2025. Moscow's air defense claimed to intercept 791 of them, with the city's mayor saying 197 were shot down over Moscow Oblast specifically. Despite the intercepts, fires broke out at the **Severnoye Domodedovo warehouse complex**, and Russian state media confirmed a Wildberries facility was damaged — the second Wildberries site hit in three days after a similar wave struck the company's largest warehouse, in Koledino, on August 16. Three people were wounded in the strikes. The same day, Russia hit back with a missile strike on a village in Ukraine's Kharkiv region, killing at least 10 civilians and wounding 17, demolishing homes in the process.
key_points: Ukraine launched **almost 800 drones** at the Moscow region overnight — its **second-largest** drone attack since January 2025
Russia says it intercepted **791 of the drones**, with **197 shot down over Moscow Oblast** alone
A **Wildberries warehouse** — Russia's biggest online retailer — caught fire for the **second time in three days** as Ukraine keeps targeting Russian logistics
**Three people were wounded** near Moscow; hours earlier a Russian missile strike killed **10 civilians** in a Kharkiv-region village
Ukraine has now hit **about a dozen Wildberries sites since July 18**, part of a deliberate campaign to disrupt Russia's supply chains

depth.background: Ukraine has spent the past year building long-range attack drones capable of reaching deep into Russia, in response to Russia's own nightly missile-and-drone barrages on Ukrainian cities. Rather than only hitting military targets, Ukraine has increasingly aimed at **logistics hubs that keep Russia's civilian economy — and war effort — running**, including warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia's version of Amazon. The goal, Ukrainian officials say, is twofold: disrupt supplies the military depends on, and erode public and economic support for the war at home. This overnight attack came just two days after a similarly sized wave of roughly 600 drones hit the same region.

stories.title: Mercedes zeroes in on Monza as the venue for Antonelli's 'inevitable' engine grid penalty
stories.what_happened: Mercedes has confirmed Antonelli is now maxed out on four distinct engine elements, meaning his next component change of any kind is an automatic 10-place grid penalty. Rather than wait for it to happen at a random race, the team is trying to choose the least costly moment to take the hit, and has settled on the Italian Grand Prix at Monza as the leading candidate — its long straights make it one of the easier tracks on the calendar to recover lost positions. Team principal Toto Wolff said Monza would be 'a good place' for Antonelli to take an engine penalty, even though Monza is also Antonelli's home race. Teammate George Russell is in a similar position on his third set of components, and Mercedes says it will decide whose penalty comes first based on team strategy, not favoritism toward Antonelli's title bid.
key_points: Antonelli is now at the **max allocation** on four separate engine parts — one more change means an automatic **10-place grid penalty**
Mercedes boss **Toto Wolff** calls Monza **'a good place'** to take the hit, since its long straights make overtaking easier
Antonelli leads the championship with **219 points**, a **50-point cushion** over Lewis Hamilton
Teammate **George Russell** faces the same dilemma; Mercedes says it **won't prioritize** Antonelli's title bid when deciding who takes a penalty first
Monza is also **Antonelli's home race**, adding pressure to how and when the team times the penalty

depth.background: F1 caps how many power-unit parts each driver can use per season — four combustion engines, four turbochargers, four exhaust systems, three energy stores, and three control electronics, among other limits. Fit one more than the allowance and the driver gets an automatic grid-position penalty, typically dropping them back about 10 places at their next race. Kimi Antonelli, a rookie in his first full title-contending season, currently leads the drivers' championship with 219 points, a 50-point lead over Lewis Hamilton, but reliability issues in the first half of the year have burned through his allotted parts faster than planned.

thread.previously: On August 17, Mercedes said both championship leader Kimi Antonelli (already on his fourth set of engine components) and George Russell (his third) would almost certainly need grid penalties in the second half of the season, and floated Monza as one possible venue for timing the hit.
thread.changed: Mercedes has now confirmed Antonelli is at the maximum allowance on four separate engine elements — the combustion engine, exhaust, energy store, and control electronics — meaning any further change triggers an automatic 10-place penalty. Team boss Toto Wolff has now specifically named the Italian Grand Prix at Monza as 'a good place' to take it, since the track's long straights make overtaking easier for a car running a fresh engine.

prev_ref.title: Mercedes says grid penalties for title leader Antonelli and George Russell are now 'almost inevitable'

stories.title: Shipping data shows Iran has lost control of the Strait of Hormuz to the US-backed Omani route
stories.what_happened: Maritime intelligence firm **Kpler** found that more than 80% of vessel transits through Hormuz over the past two weeks took the UN-authorized Omani route rather than the path Iran claims to control, according to CNN Business reporting. That shift has stopped Iran from charging tolls on shipping through the strait, something it was still doing as recently as spring. Iran has attacked ships attempting the Omani route, but most vessels are now crossing anyway, trusting **US naval forces** to protect them. "It increasingly looks like Iran has at least partially lost control of the strait," said Kpler's head of crude oil analysis, Homayoun Falakshahi. Separately, Oman and Iran are holding talks to restore normal freedom of navigation through the strait on their own terms — without US involvement — a prospect reports say frustrates Trump.
key_points: More than **80% of ships** crossing the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks used the Omani route, not Iran's, per tracking firm Kpler.
Iran can no longer collect **tolls** on strait traffic, cutting off a revenue stream it relied on during the standoff.
Analysts say Iran has "**at least partially lost control**" of the world's most important oil chokepoint.
Iran has attacked ships taking the Omani route, but most now cross anyway, betting on **US naval protection**.
Oman and Iran are quietly negotiating to restore free navigation **without the US involved** — a move Trump reportedly dislikes.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow shipping lane between Iran and Oman that roughly **a fifth of the world's oil** passes through every day — there is no practical way around it for tankers leaving the Gulf. The current standoff escalated after a 60-day US-Iran ceasefire deadline expired without a deal, Trump claimed the strait as effectively **US-controlled territory**, and Iran responded by declaring a "fully offensive" policy to enforce its own claim over the waterway, attacking ships that used the rival route past Oman's coast.

stories.title: India's biggest IT firms shed nearly 7,000 jobs this year as AI forces a hiring reset
stories.what_happened: A Business Standard review of FY26 hiring data shows India's five largest IT companies posted a combined headcount contraction of **6,981 employees**, compared with an increase of 12,798 the year before — a sharp reversal driven largely by roughly **23,000 job cuts at TCS** and slower growth elsewhere. A separate Nomura study tracking AI's employment impact since 2023 found the country added 83,100 AI-related roles against about 32,900 jobs lost to AI adoption, meaning AI has been a net job creator so far — but the study also found the new roles rarely go to the same people whose jobs were automated away. More than half the IT firms surveyed said entry-level and junior positions have specifically shrunk over the past two years, as AI tools absorb routine coding, testing and support work that used to be how graduates got their start. In response, companies are pivoting from external hiring toward large-scale internal reskilling programs, even as a shortage of AI-ready talent makes specialist recruitment slower and more expensive.
key_points: India's top five IT firms — **TCS, Infosys, HCL Tech, Wipro, and Tech Mahindra** — together cut headcount by **6,981 jobs** in FY26, versus adding nearly 12,800 the year before.
A Nomura study found India created **83,100 AI-related jobs** since 2023 but lost roughly **32,900** to AI — a net gain, but in different roles than the ones it destroyed.
**55% of IT companies** say entry-level hiring has shrunk over the last two years, as AI tools take over junior coding and support work.
Firms are shifting from mass hiring to **reskilling at scale**, retraining existing staff instead of only recruiting new AI talent.
A shortage of "industry-ready" AI specialists is slowing the rebound even as demand for AI skills rises.

depth.background: India's IT services industry has for decades been the country's biggest white-collar job engine, hiring hundreds of thousands of engineering graduates every year on the promise of steady, predictable growth. That model is now colliding with generative AI tools that can write, test, and debug code — tasks that used to be the entry point for fresh graduates. Industry leaders like TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCL Tech and Tech Mahindra have spent much of 2026 talking publicly about "AI-first" strategies while simultaneously trimming headcount for the first time in years.

stories.title: Trump orders US troops to scale back drills with South Korea, saying Seoul wouldn't help with his Iran war
stories.what_happened: On Sunday, Trump announced in a social media post that he was ordering the Pentagon to **'substantially reduce'** joint exercises with South Korea, saying the drills are costly and send a **'totally inappropriate and hostile'** signal to North Korea, which he described as having been **'unthreatening and respectful'** during his presidency. He said the decision followed South Korea's refusal to actively join his push to denuclearize Iran, and he pointed to his rapport with North Korean leader **Kim Jong Un** as a further reason to ease up. The announcement came just as US and South Korean troops began this week's Ulchi Freedom Shield exercise, designed specifically to sharpen readiness against a North Korean attack. South Korea's foreign ministry said it hoped the warmer Trump-Kim relationship could **'pave the way'** for actual talks between Washington and Pyongyang. President Lee Jae Myung, at a cabinet meeting the next day, called for South Korea to build **stronger independent defense capabilities**, while insisting the allied drills were purely defensive and not aimed at provoking the North.
key_points: Trump told Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to **'substantially reduce'** the annual joint US-South Korea military exercises.
He said South Korea had **declined to help** the US effort to denuclearize Iran.
Trump cited his **'very good' relationship with Kim Jong Un** as another reason for the pullback.
The order landed just as **Ulchi Freedom Shield**, the allies' biggest annual drill, was starting.
South Korea's President **Lee Jae Myung** responded by calling for stronger **independent** national defense.

depth.background: The US has stationed troops in South Korea since the **1950-53 Korean War** ended in an armistice, not a peace treaty, and the two countries still hold large joint military drills every year to keep their forces ready against North Korea. Those drills, including this week's Ulchi Freedom Shield, are the clearest daily proof that Washington's defense promise to Seoul is real. Trump has separately been leading a US military campaign pressuring Iran to give up its nuclear program, including threats around the **Strait of Hormuz**, and has been asking allies around the world to back that effort.

stories.title: Red Bull's junior program has three drivers fighting for one seat — and it's about to get messier
stories.what_happened: Lawson and Lindblad, both out of contract at Racing Bulls at the end of 2026, are being pushed into direct competition for whichever Red Bull-family seat opens up next, with team principal Alan Permane telling them they're free to race wheel-to-wheel with one condition: don't make contact. On competitive form, Lawson currently holds the upper hand, sitting 9th in the drivers' championship on 43 points against Lindblad's 23 points in 11th, and leads their head-to-head qualifying battle 6-5. But the picture isn't clean: Lindblad is actually marginally quicker on average lap time. Complicating things further, Formula 2 championship leader **Nikola Tsolov**, a 19-year-old Bulgarian and fellow Red Bull junior, is pushing hard for his own F1 opportunity. Tsolov is set to get his first real taste of a Formula 1 car in a Racing Bulls test at Imola on August 27, driving a 2025-specification car under rules that let him bank the superlicence points needed to eventually race in F1 — he currently has 25 of the 40 points required.
key_points: Racing Bulls teammates **Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad** are both out of contract at the end of 2026 and effectively racing each other for the next Red Bull opening.

That system has been unusually brutal this year — Red Bull has swapped drivers in and out of its senior seat repeatedly, and Lawson himself was demoted from the senior team early in the season after a rocky start, landing back at Racing Bulls. With Max Verstappen's own contract situation also unresolved, the driver most likely to get the next opening at either team is whoever wins the internal fight happening right now at Racing Bulls.

stories.title: Meta's $1.4 trillion child-safety trial opens with a bipartisan coalition of states accusing it of engineering Instagram to hook kids
stories.what_happened: Opening arguments began on August 18 in a landmark federal trial pitting Meta against a bipartisan coalition of **29 US states**, with lawyers for **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** leading the case. They allege Meta deliberately engineered Instagram and Facebook features — **infinite scroll, photo filters, and the 'like' button** — to be compulsively addictive for minors, and that it collected data from children under 13 without parental consent, violating child privacy law. Meta's defense rejects the claims, pointing to years of investment in teen safety tools like age checks and screen-time limits. The financial stakes are enormous: potential penalties have been estimated as high as **$1.4 trillion**, close to Meta's entire Nasdaq market value, though any final number would likely be far lower after negotiation or appeal. This builds on precedent — a New Mexico court already ordered Meta to pay **$567 million**, on top of an earlier $375 million fine, over similar child-safety allegations.
key_points: **29 US states** are suing Meta; opening arguments from **California, Colorado, Kentucky and New Jersey** kicked off the trial in federal court.
States allege Meta built **Instagram and Facebook** to be addictive to minors using **infinite scroll, filters, and the 'like' button**, and collected data from under-13s without parental consent.
The potential penalty is estimated as high as **$1.4 trillion** — roughly equal to Meta's **entire market value** on the Nasdaq.
Meta says it has **spent years building teen protections** and denies deliberately designing addictive products.
A **New Mexico court already fined Meta $567 million** this year on top of an earlier $375 million child-safety penalty — a preview of the financial risk here.

depth.background: For several years, whistleblower leaks and internal research (like the 2021 Facebook Papers) have alleged that Meta knew its platforms could harm teen mental health but prioritized engagement and growth anyway. That evidence fed a wave of state lawsuits, and this case — a bipartisan coalition of 29 states, with four leading the opening arguments — is the biggest test yet of whether Meta can be held financially liable for how it designed its apps. The case matters far beyond Meta: a loss could set a legal template for regulating addictive app design across the whole tech industry.

stories.title: Russia knocks out a major Ukrainian power plant in its 230th strike on the same site, part of a 147-drone night ahead of winter
stories.what_happened: On August 18, Russian forces struck one of DTEK's thermal power plants so heavily that it was forced to **completely halt electricity generation**; DTEK didn't disclose the plant's location for security reasons but confirmed **significant equipment damage**. It was the **230th attack** on DTEK's thermal plants since the war began. The strike was part of a wider night of bombardment: Ukraine's air force said Russia fired **147 drones**, of which **111 were shot down or jammed**, while a separate missile strike on **Pechenihy** in Kharkiv Oblast killed at least **10 civilians** and injured others. DTEK said no plant employees were hurt and repair crews were mobilizing immediately alongside national grid operator Ukrenergo to keep the wider system stable.
key_points: A Russian strike forced one of **DTEK's thermal power plants** to completely **halt electricity generation**, with equipment severely damaged.

**No plant staff were injured**, but DTEK says repair crews are already coordinating with grid operator **Ukrenergo**.

depth.background: **DTEK** is Ukraine's largest private energy company, running thermal power plants that keep millions of homes and businesses supplied through the country's brutal winters. Since Russia's invasion, Moscow has repeatedly targeted Ukraine's power grid in the cold months, trying to freeze the country into concessions by knocking out heat and electricity rather than only fighting on the front line. This has happened before: past winters saw rolling blackouts across Ukraine after waves of strikes on exactly this kind of infrastructure.

stories.title: Verstappen reportedly wants only a one-year Red Bull deal, resisting the team's push to erase his exit clause

Red Bull's new offer is widely seen as an attempt to lock him down long-term and remove that flexibility before it becomes a problem.

stories.title: An Israeli strike kills at least six in Gaza City as Kushner's talks with Netanyahu fail to revive a US ceasefire plan

Israel's military said the strike targeted commanders and operatives of Hamas's elite **Nukhba force** while they were meeting at the site. The strike came the same day Kushner held talks with Netanyahu in an effort to get Israel to implement a US-backed ceasefire framework that **Hamas had already agreed to** — but the meeting ended with **no agreement**. stories.title: Trump claims the Strait of Hormuz as 'new' US territory and rules out extending Iran's ceasefire deadline
stories.what_happened: President Trump escalated the standoff on Tuesday by posting a map that labels the Strait of Hormuz as **'new' US territory** — a claim with no legal basis, since the strait runs through Iranian and Omani territorial waters under international law. He simultaneously said **no negotiations with Iran are underway or scheduled**, a day after his own administration said it had opened an informal channel with Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). Iran's government accused Washington of using the deadline's expiry to **'squeeze' concessions** out of Tehran rather than negotiate in good faith. A senior Iranian official told Reuters that, with diplomacy stalled, Iran would consider a **'timely and precise' military strike** aimed at breaking the US naval blockade around the strait if it has to.
key_points: Trump posted a map labeling the **Strait of Hormuz** as **'new' US territory**, an unprecedented claim over a waterway that has never been US soil.
He said **no talks are taking place** with Iran, contradicting his own administration's claim just a day earlier of a **back-channel with the IRGC**.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters Iran will launch a **'timely and precise' military strike** to break the US naval blockade if diplomacy keeps failing.
The **60-day ceasefire negotiation window** with Iran expired this week with **no agreement reached**.

depth.background: The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow chokepoint between Iran and Oman that ships must pass through to move oil out of the Persian Gulf — it is the world's single most important oil transit route. A **temporary US-Iran ceasefire**, reached after weeks of naval and drone confrontations, gave both sides a **60-day window** to negotiate a lasting deal; that window expired this week without one. In the days since, Iran has seized a UAE-owned tanker, an unidentified projectile struck another vessel in the strait, and Iran formally declared a shift to a **'fully offensive' military posture**.

stories.title: Babar Azam ruled out of the Headingley Test with a hand injury — Salman Ali Agha steps in as Pakistan captain

stories.title: A Chinese robotaxi startup just lined up more than 4,000 self-driving cars for cities outside China

CEO James Peng framed the milestone as proof the company can scale internationally by plugging into partners' existing apps rather than building demand city by city on its own.

stories.title: Cadillac names Marcin Budkowski team principal, hours after abruptly sacking founding boss Graeme Lowdon
